Instruction on the Perfection of Wisdom.
II 5 <Homage to the Three Jewels> ||
Homage to the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara.
III.1.1.1 That which shines upon the heads of the perfected ones like the pollen of the flowers offered at the gateway to liberation.
Victorious is that dust from the feet of the One Possessing Ten Powers, which is sought by the crowns of the gods. || 1 ||

III.1.2.1 The liberations of other proponents are but partial aspects of existence; the destruction of existence is the liberation of the Śrāvakas, which is imperishable. Having transcended both nirvāṇa and existence, the eternal, supreme state of the Sugata is the ultimate consummation of mastery. (3)

III.1.2.2 Just as a copper vessel, though impure, may be surpassed by a crystal that is inferior [in quality], yet the sun among the stars excels because of its radiance; so too, among those who possess tranquility, the Buddha is distinguished by his awakening and his weighty qualities. (4)

III.1.2.3 To the one who cuts off existence, who removes faults, who is an ocean of virtues, and who is always the sole cause of welfare for the world— to him, the wise, casting aside inferior positions,
aspire for unsurpassed enlightenment.
III.1.3.1 Through the method of the perfections (*pāramitānaya*), awakening bears fruit only after a long time due to the afflictions (*kleśa*);
through the method of mantra (*mantranaya*), awakening is attained swiftly without afflictions at all. Herein, the first path belongs to those possessing the power of unrestrained splendor.
But for those who have accomplished an abundance of faith, there is the other path.
III.1.3.2 I consider him alone to be fortunate among sages who exerts himself for awakening, though it is exceedingly difficult for a very long time;
he who knows the mantras that swiftly bestow that very state through ease—he alone is a Sugata, a jewel of the Sugatas. (7)
III.1.4 20 He accomplishes the mantras; the five perfections are in the palm of his hand—he who meditates day by day on the Blessed Lady, the supreme perfection.

III.2 Here, one who has taken sole refuge in the Three Jewels, who is faithful and compassionate, who has generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), who has undertaken the bodhisattva vows, and who— having accumulated the provisions for their sake— now seeks realization, develops the wisdom consisting of hearing and the wisdom consisting of reflection.
Having understood the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā, one should cultivate it.

III.3 Therein, having correctly heard from [the Bodhisattvapiṭaka], [the Prajñāpāramitā, etc.], or from one or another sūtra, or from various portions of sūtras collected right here; or having himself inferred something in some respect;
or [having mastered] the means for establishing the relationship between word and meaning, both in terms of the phrasing and the meaning—
Certainty and retention constitute the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*).

III.4 10 When one who is alone and in seclusion correctly investigates that very same object through reasoning, and regarding the truth and reality of that object, arrives at the definitive certainty—through the means of reasoning—that "it is exactly thus and not otherwise," that is the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).

III.5.1 15. Here, in brief, phenomena (*dharma*) are to be known by way of two aspects of reality: first, by way of their extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), meaning that they are just this many; and second, by way of their mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), meaning that they are just like this. We shall explain these two in due order.
III.5.2.1 20. It was said by the Blessed One: “O Brahmin, ‘everything, everything’ refers only to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Among these, form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) are the six object-elements (*viṣaya-dhātu*), from the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) up to the mental-object-element (*dharma-dhātu*). The eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are the six faculty-elements (*indriya-dhātu*), from the eye-element (*cakṣu-dhātu*) up to the mind-element (*manas-dhātu*). Following from the connection with the faculties, there are the six consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*), beginning with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣur-vijñāna-dhātu*)...
The element of consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness.

III.5.2.3 Thus there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The first eleven elements are the eleven bases (*āyatana*), from the base of form (*rūpāyatana*) up to the base of the body (*kāyāyatana*). The remaining seven elements constitute the single mind-base (*mana-āyatana*), namely, from the mind-element (*manodhātu*) up to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).

III.5.2.4 Thus are the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). The five objects, the five sense faculties, and the form included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*) constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). From the base of mental phenomena, two mental factors constitute two aggregates: the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). The remaining mental factors and the formations dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) constitute the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), however, is not subsumed under the aggregates at all, because the meaning of "aggregate" does not apply to it.
Thus, "the five aggregates" refers to the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection regarding the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*).

III.5.3.1 The Buddha, the Blessed One, is the supreme authority (*pramāṇa*). This is because he has abandoned all defects along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanā*), because he possesses the highest excellence of all virtues, because he always and in every way correctly perceives all objects of knowledge, and because all his undertakings are for the sake of others. Therefore, whatever has been spoken by the Tathāgata is exactly so and not otherwise.
And this is because the masters who know the reality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatattva*) have refuted the doctrines of others.
[It is] exactly that.

III.5.3.2.1 Furthermore, [the opponents] maintain that entities are indeed non-momentary; for this very reason, they do not exist. For existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity (*śakti*) for some effect;

for that which is incapable of producing anything is no different from a horse’s horn. And capacity is the functional nature (*svabhāva*) of the potent, which is of the form of "acting" (*kurvadrūpa*). Moreover, the nature of a non-momentary entity is exactly the same before as it is after. If that [nature] were capable of some effect, then it would have been capable even previously, and later—

It would have to be capable [of action]. And consequently, it follows that it performs that effect both before and after; yet that is untenable, because it is impossible to perform what has already been performed. Therefore, the nature of a non-momentary entity is simply incapable. And that which is incapable is non-existent, like the horn of a donkey. Thus, the non-momentary does not exist; therefore, the positions of the opponents [are untenable].
[All] phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature.
III.5.3.2.2 Furthermore, even that which is asserted by certain others to be momentary, such as the flame of cognition (*buddhi*),
is asserted by them to be connected precisely with the non-momentary; therefore, it is refuted along with the refutation of the non-momentary.

III.5.3.2.3 Now, others might also maintain that everything is momentary; however, the authors of the treatises do not say this. Here, it is the opinions of the authors of the treatises that are being examined, not those of mere individuals, because of their infinite number and because omniscience is absolutely impossible among them. Therefore, "all" consists only of this: namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*)—this is the investigation regarding the extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) by means of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).

III.5.4.1.1 There is much that must be said regarding the Mahāyāna as a whole; however, we shall speak in brief, having collected from various sections of the sūtras both the meaning and the phrasing in some places, and the meaning alone in others.

III.5.4.1.2 Here, four reliances have been taught by the Blessed One for the sake of the non-confusion of those to be trained. They are as follows: one should rely on the Dharma and not rely on the person; one should rely on the meaning and not rely on the letter; one should rely on sūtras of definitive meaning and not rely on sūtras of interpretable meaning; one should rely on direct knowledge and not rely on discursive consciousness.

The meaning established by the Tathāgata or by a Bodhisattva and others is authoritative, whereas that which is falsely conceived by anyone else is not. Wisdom (*jñāna*) is authoritative, not discursive consciousness (*vijñāna*).

III.5.4.1.3.2 III.5.4.1.3.1 The explanation of these [points] is found in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra* and other treatises: the Dharma taught by the Teacher is the authority, not the person who rejects it; the intended meaning is the authority, not the literal expression when the meaning is not intended. Regarding the Tathāgata—
In this context, "knowledge" (jñāna) is supramundane, non-conceptual wisdom (prajñā), while "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the conceptual wisdom consisting of what has been heard and so forth.

By means of the first reliance—reliance on the Dharma—one does not lose one's resolve regarding the meaning of the Dharma. By means of the second, one personally investigates the intended meaning through reasoning. By means of the third, one hears from others the method of that non-erroneous meaning. By means of the fourth...
It is not from supramundane knowledge.
III.5.4.1.5.1 Regarding the third reliance (*pratisaraṇa*): that which is definitive (*nītārtha*) has been explained; that which is interpretable (*neyārtha*) remains to be explained.

A sūtra whose meaning is to be grasped according to the underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) and not according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*) is one of interpretable meaning; it is so called because its meaning is to be led [to the definitive]. By what means is it of interpretable meaning? By means of reasoning (*yukti*) and through explanatory sūtras of definitive meaning. For example, the *Arthaviniścaya-sūtra* [is definitive] because it speaks of external objects; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [is definitive] because it speaks of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). This...
For it is not to be led [to that meaning] by other sūtras, because those [sūtras] lead to it otherwise.
"Those very same dharmas which are in the Śrāvakayāna are of the single flavor of suchness (tathatā) in the Mahāyāna; therefore, there is the state of a single vehicle (ekayānatā).
This is because of the statement in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.

"The vehicle of the path is also one because of the commonality of selflessness; the vehicle of the fruit is also one because of the commonality of liberation; therefore, there is a single vehicle. From such statements in other sūtras, even that which is the prophecy for śrāvakas therein is to be interpreted as referring to those śrāvakas who are directed toward awakening, and not to those whose sole aim is tranquility.
Thus, because it is stated in other sūtras, and as it is said in the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*):

"Sentient beings of diverse lineages (*gotra*) are seen with diverse intentions (*āśaya*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), inclinations (*adhimukti*), and faculties (*indriya*). According to their lineage, they strive by means of the three vehicles and attain the three types of enlightenment. However, one who lacks a lineage (*agotraka*), striving through both wholesome and unwholesome [actions], [remains in] saṃsāra..."

It is indeed like dross. Just as when ores such as iron, copper, and so forth—whether belonging to a specific lineage (*gotra*) or lacking one—are smelted, there arises dross consisting of iron, copper, silver, or gold; likewise, even if all the Buddhas were to assemble, they would not be able to cause a *śrāvaka* who is solely intent on tranquility to realize unexcelled perfect enlightenment, nor could they bring to final nirvana a sentient being who lacks the spiritual lineage (*agotraka*). Thus it is said.

III.5.4.1.5.2 That sūtra whose meaning is exclusively definitive (*nītārtha*) and does not exist according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*) because there is no second meaning—that is a sūtra of definitive meaning, on the grounds that its meaning is indeed definitive. By what is it of definitive meaning? Either by that very sūtra itself, or by another, or by both. Which is by that very sūtra itself? The *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*, the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*, and so forth. Which is by another? The *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā* and so forth. Which is by both? The *Āryapañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā* and so forth.

For in that *Dharmakāyaparivarta*, there is an explanation of the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) which has the function of establishing non-perversion. This indeed has the characteristic of causing the abandonment of those perversions characterized by adherence to the literal meaning. Furthermore, that which has been established as definitive (*nīta*) by the Tathāgata or by Bodhisattvas and others authorized by him must not be interpreted otherwise by others, because the Blessed One alone is the supreme authority and to avoid the consequence of an infinite regress.

III.5.4.2.1 There are four intentions (*abhiprāya*) and four underlying purposes (*abhisaṃdhi*) of the Tathāgata regarding his teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). These are: the intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*), the intention of another time (*kālāntarābhiprāya*), the intention of another meaning (*arthāntarābhiprāya*), and the intention regarding the disposition of individuals (*pudgalāśayābhiprāya*). Furthermore, there are: the underlying purpose of introduction (*avatāraṇābhisaṃdhi*), the underlying purpose of counteraction (*pratipakṣābhisaṃdhi*), the underlying purpose of characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisaṃdhi*), and the underlying purpose of transformation (*pariṇāmanābhisaṃdhi*). In this context, that by which a meaning is led according to what one wishes to express is the "intention" (*abhiprāya*); that which serves as the specific purpose within the sound of the teaching is the "underlying purpose" (*abhisaṃdhi*).
III.5.4.2.2.1 Therein, the intention of equality is as follows: "At that time, I myself was that Tathāgata Vipaśyin. This is by way of the equality of the *dharmakāya*. Thus it is said.
[To you].

III.5.4.2.2.2 Intention regarding another time (*kālāntarābhiprāya*): For example, "Those who shall make a vow for Sukhāvatī will be reborn there," or "By grasping the name of the Tathāgata Vimalacandraprabha, one becomes fixed in unsurpassed, perfect awakening (*anuttarāyāṃ samyaksambodhau*). The meaning is that it refers to another time.

The intention of equality (*samatābhiprāya*) is as stated: "At that time, I myself was the perfectly awakened one (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) Vipaśyin," because there is no distinction in the *dharmakāya*. [MSABh XII.18.1] Furthermore, it is said: "Those who make a vow for Sukhāvatī will be reborn there," and "By the mere grasping of the name of the Tathāgata Vimalacandraprabha, one becomes fixed in unsurpassed perfect awakening (*anuttarāyāṃ samyaksambodhau*). [MSABh XII.19-23]

III.5.4.2.2.3 The intention of another meaning is as follows: "After attending upon Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, realization arises in the Mahāyāna. The underlying sense is that "realization" refers to the penetration of the dharmadhātu.

III.5.4.2.2.4 Intention regarding the disposition of individuals (*pudgalāśayābhiprāya*): For example, one may disparage a certain teaching to someone while praising it to another. Such a desire to speak in that manner arises in accordance with their dispositions, for the sake of causing one who is satisfied with a single [teaching] to adopt a second.

III.5.4.2.3.1 The intention of introduction (*avatāraṇābhisandhi*) is as follows: [the teaching that] "there is a spontaneously born being" and "there exist forms, sounds, and so forth. This is for the purpose of introducing those who fear the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) into the Teaching, respectively.
III.5.4.2.3.2 The intentional teaching regarding the counteragent (pratipakṣābhisandhi) will be explained, for example, in the *Dhāraṇī of the Two Verses*.
The imagined, the dependent, and the perfected [natures] are mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating that all phenomena, respectively, do not exist, are like illusions, and are equal to space.
III.5.4.2.3.4 The intentionality of dedication is as follows—

The intention regarding characteristics (*lakṣaṇābhisandhi*) is as follows: "Form does not exist," up to "the Buddha-dharmas do not exist"; "form is like an illusion," up to "the Buddha-dharmas are like an illusion"; "form is equal to space," up to "the Buddha-dharmas are equal to space"—these are the characteristics. [Regarding] the three natures (*trayaḥ svabhāvāḥ*), those who perceive the essential in the non-essential...
Firmly established in perversion and thoroughly afflicted by the afflictions, they attain supreme enlightenment.

Thus, the transformation of syllables is for the sake of profundity. And in this regard, it should be transformed as follows: "The concentration of the mind is essence-less and non-dispersive; yet they perceive an essence therein. There is a perversion regarding worldly grasping, thinking that what is impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self is 'self' and 'mine'; yet they are well-established therein. Affliction is the exhaustion from long and difficult exertion;
yet they are excessively tormented by it."

III.5.4.2.3.5 Disrespect for the Buddha and the Dharma, laziness, contentment with a mere trifle, conduct characterized by passion and pride, remorse, and instability— these constitute the divisions [of the indeterminate]. ||6||
The obscuration of sentient beings and its antidote is the teaching of the Supreme Vehicle;
from that, the abandonment of all faults that constitute obstacles occurs for them.
(7) Thus it is said.
In the *Śatasāhasrikā Vaipulyasūtra*, there is a dhāraṇī consisting of two verses; for therein, the two verses constitute the root, while the three verses constitute the benefit.
This verse is also cited in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya* (MSABh XII.19).

[MSA XII.20] For bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage (*aniyatagotra*), turning away from the Mahāyāna constitutes the differentiation of the indeterminate. The abandonment of that [turning away] is for the sake of maintaining bodhisattvas in the Mahāyāna and for the sake of attracting śrāvakas. The discourse on the supreme vehicle (*agrayānasambhāṣā*) is the teaching of the Mahāyāna. The obstacles are those very eight hindrances, beginning with contempt for the Buddha. Among these, the discourse on the supreme vehicle is the antidote to the hindrance of contempt for the Buddha.

For example, it is as when I myself said to him, "Not at the proper time," referring to [the Buddhas] from Vipaśyin up to Kāśyapa. Regarding the obscuration of contempt for the Dharma, it is as previously stated: "as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Regarding the obscuration of laziness, it is as previously stated: "those who [are reborn] in Sukhāvatī" and "Vimalacandraprabha. Regarding the obscuration of being satisfied with only a little, it is where the Blessed One in some places disparages giving and so forth, while in other places he has praised them.

Regarding the obscuration of conduct characterized by passion (*rāga*), [the Buddha] describes the splendor of a particular buddha-field. Regarding the obscuration of conduct characterized by pride (*māna*), he describes the superior excellence of a certain buddha. Regarding the obscuration of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), he says: "All those who commit harm against the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall go to heaven. Regarding the obscuration of indeterminate division (*aniyata-bheda*), there is the prophecy of the great śrāvakas regarding their future Buddhahood and the teaching of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) with the statement: "There is no second vehicle. In these cases, the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) is the desire to eliminate the obscuration.

III.5.4.3.1 In the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other [sūtras], three natures (*svabhāva*) are taught: the imagined (*parikalpita*), the dependent (*paratantra*), and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*). These very same [natures] are taught in the *Bhagavatī* (the *Prajñāpāramitā*) under the heading of "establishment in non-perversion" as the imagined form, the conceptualized form, and the true nature (*dharmatā*) of form, up to the Buddha-qualities.
Thus it is said.

III.5.4.3.2 The detailed exposition of their characteristics and so forth is found in the sūtras; here, however, we shall state it in brief. That intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena which is imagined through mental chatter associated with names is their *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), because it does not exist according to its own characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). For example: "form," "sound," "eye," "ear," and so forth. But that [nature], in brief, is twofold: the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).
Thus.

III.5.4.3.3 Furthermore, that consciousness which arises even when duality does not exist—appearing as duality through the power of the latencies of attachment to the imagined nature—and which does not arise when that [attachment] is abandoned, is the dependent nature (*paratantra*) of all phenomena, because it is dependent upon causes and conditions.

III.5.4.3.4 Furthermore, that which is the emptiness, seclusion, and absence of that dependent nature (paratantra) at all times due to that imagined nature (parikalpita)—this is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) of all phenomena; it is established as absolute because it exists exactly as such at all times. For there is no phenomenon whatsoever, anywhere or at any time, that is not empty of duality. Nor is there any variety in that emptiness, because it is always and everywhere of a single flavor, like space.

For space, because its characteristic is the absence of form, is always and everywhere of a single flavor; likewise, emptiness also, because its characteristic is the absence of duality. Therefore, it is called the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

III.5.4.3.5 Among these, the first exists as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*), because it is perceived by the foolish in that very way; it does not exist substantially (*dravyasat*), nor does it exist ultimately (*paramārthasat*). The second exists substantially because it is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*); it does not exist as a conceptual designation. The third exists ultimately because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) for purification; this is on the grounds that it is an objective support for purification and not for affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Even the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), when taken as an objective support in its perfected form (*pariniṣpanna-rūpa*), becomes something that exists ultimately.

However, when apprehended by means of an imagined form (*parikalpita-rūpa*), it exists only as a conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-sat*), because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) for affliction; that is to say, an objective support for affliction does not lead to purification.

III.5.4.3.6.1 The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) alone is called "unreal imagination" (*abhūta-parikalpa*). This is because unreal things are imagined within it, or because by means of it one imagines what is unreal. As the Blessed One Maitreya said: "The imagined and the dependent..."
And it is indeed the perfected nature.

From the object and from the unreal imagination, the unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms. Among these, the perception of the object is consciousness, while the perception of its specific qualities consists of the mental factors. (9)
"And because of the non-existence of duality, it is taught.

(8) This, moreover, refers to the mind and mental factors of the three realms. In that context, the apprehension of the intrinsic nature of objects is the mind (*citta*), while the apprehensions of their specific qualities are the mental factors (*caitta*). As it has been said:

And unreal imagination consists of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms. Among these, the perception of an object is consciousness, while the perception of its specific qualities consists of the mental factors.
Thus it is said.

III.5.4.3.6.2 Furthermore, it is threefold: the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Among these, it is called "storehouse" (*ālaya*) because it is the substratum for the latencies (*vāsanā*) of all defiled phenomena; it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it perceives its own nature. It is "afflicted" (*kliṣṭa*) because it is always associated with these four afflictions: self-delusion (*ātmamoha*), self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātmasneha*), and self-pride (*ātmamāna*); it is called "mind" (*manas*) because its essential nature is the constant cogitation of "I."

Activity arises from repeated cultivation; consciousness arises from the apprehension of objects. Among these, the first [the storehouse-consciousness] manifests as the environment, enjoyment, and the body: the "environment" is the receptacle world; "enjoyment" refers to the five sense-objects; and the "body" refers to the five sense-faculties. Its manifestation is its taking on those forms. The active consciousness consists of the six groups of consciousness.

Furthermore, the unreal imagination is fourfold, which is the fourfold consciousness: namely, that which appears as objects, that which appears as sentient beings, that which appears as a self, and that which appears as representations. Among these, the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which appears as the locus and the experience [of the world], is that which appears as objects. That which appears as the body is that which appears as sentient beings. That which is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) is that which appears as a self, because it grasps the storehouse-consciousness itself as a self.
That which is the evolving consciousness is the manifestation of representation, because it appears as the grasper of objects.

Furthermore, the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is twofold and sixfold. How is it twofold? It consists of the characteristic of the grasped (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of the grasper (*grāhaka-lakṣaṇa*), because they manifest as the state of being grasped and the state of being a grasper. How is it sixfold? Because each of those two is threefold: namely, that which manifests as the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and body (*deha*); and [the three consisting of] mind (*manas*), apprehension (*udgraha*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Among these, "mind" is the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*). "Apprehension" refers to the five active consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
"Conceptualization" is the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), because it is exclusively conceptualizing in nature.

Furthermore, the false imagination is of eight kinds: the eight groups of consciousness, namely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), and the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

III.5.4.3.7.1 That which is unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*) is itself all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*), all affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and all cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). However, that which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of that very same unreal imagination. By what is it empty? It is empty of duality—that is, of the imagined (*parikalpita*) apprehended object (*grāhya*) and apprehending subject (*grāhaka*). The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of that emptiness is the non-existence of duality within that unreal imagination, and the existence of that non-existence of duality.

Since this emptiness is the non-existence of duality, it is therefore not an entity (*bhāva*); since it is the existence of that non-existence of duality, it is therefore not a non-entity (*abhāva*). And it is said in the *Ārya-saṃdhinirmocana* and other scriptures: "It is neither non-different from the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), nor is it different.
For if it were non-different from them, then fools who perceive those conditioned factors would [perceive] emptiness..."

Those who perceive it thus would become those who have seen the truth; they would be Arhats, up to and including Perfectly Awakened Buddhas. Furthermore, just as conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are defilement (*saṃkleśa*), so too would emptiness (*śūnyatā*) be defilement. And since that [emptiness] is eternal, defilement would be eternal. Moreover, just as emptiness is undifferentiated among all conditioned phenomena, so too their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be undifferentiated. Furthermore, yogins do not seek any reality higher than emptiness.
Thus, they would not seek any reality other than the specific characteristics of the conditioned formations;
therefore, it is not something other than them.

Nor is it something other. Why? Because it is merely their own selflessness (nairātmyamātra), merely their lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatāmātra), just as whiteness is in a conch shell. Furthermore, if it were other than them, then even for those who have seen the truth, the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāranimitta) would not have ceased.

That would be the case; consequently, they would not be liberated from the bondage of signs and the bondage of depravity. Therefore, for them there would be neither nirvāṇa nor perfect awakening. Furthermore, this [emptiness] would not be the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). Moreover, defilement and purification would both be established as having distinct characteristics simultaneously. Therefore, it is not something other than those [conditioned phenomena].
As it is said:

"The non-existence of duality is indeed the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness. It is neither existence nor non-existence, neither diverse nor of a single characteristic. (10)
This is the characteristic of emptiness.

III.5.4.3.7.2 5 Now, its synonyms are: suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the signless (*ānimitta*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Now, the meaning of the synonyms: It is *tathatā* (suchness) because, being changeless, it remains exactly so at all times. The *bhūtas* are the *tattvas* (realities); their *koṭi* (limit) is their pinnacle, hence *bhūtakoṭi*. There are no signs (*nimittas*) in this, thus it is *animitta*; the suffix *-aṇ* is used in its own sense (*svārthe*), and it is called *animitta* because, upon the subsiding of all signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), that [state] is perceived. It is the object (*artha*) or domain (*viṣaya*) of the supreme (*parama*) supramundane knowledge, thus it is *paramārtha*. The *dharmas* are the noble qualities (*āryadharma*); their *dhātu* is their cause. By means of that objective support (*ālambana*), they [the noble qualities] arise.
*patter* is the *dharmadhātu*; the state (*bhāva*) or nature (*prakṛti*) of phenomena (*dharma*) is their *dharmatā*.

III.5.4.3.7.3 Now, its divisions: previously, it is both afflicted (*kliṣṭā*) and stained (*samalā*), because it is not identical [to those stains] due to adventitious stains of obscuration. Later, when those are abandoned by means of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), it becomes pure (*viśuddhā*) and stainless (*nirmalā*). Just as the purification of the water-element, gold, and space occurs through the removal of adventitious impurities such as dust, copper-colored tarnish, and frost; therefore, this [nature] is not truly defiled.

The non-existence of duality is indeed the existence of that non-existence; this is the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnya*). It is neither existence nor non-existence, nor is it characterized by difference or identity.

The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not impure, because the mind is luminous by nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*); yet it is neither undefiled nor pure, due to its association with adventitious defilements. As it is said: "It is both afflicted and purified."

It is both stained and stainless; its purity is held to be like the purification of the element of water, gold, and space. (11) If it were not defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated; if it were not pure, spiritual practice would be fruitless. (12) It is neither defiled nor non-defiled.
And it is neither pure nor impure, because the mind is luminous by nature and afflictions are adventitious. (13.15)
III.5.4.3.8 Eight consciousnesses have been mentioned. Among them, which one proceeds in what manner? Or at what time?

What is it? First, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome karmas in a happy destiny and of unwholesome karmas in an unhappy destiny. When the maturation of prior karma has been exhausted, it is produced by the latencies of karma accompanied by the latencies of the adherence to the grasped and the grasper. Once produced, it proceeds like a torrential stream for as long as life lasts. Thereafter, it arises again in another [life] in the same manner and proceeds as a stream. And it was said by the Blessed One: "If this were not defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated."
If it were already pure, effort would be fruitless.
It is neither afflicted nor unafflicted, and it is neither pure nor impure;
for the mind is luminous by nature and the afflictions are adventitious.
Thus:
"The appropriating consciousness is profound and subtle; like a torrent, it flows containing all seeds. I have not revealed this to the foolish, lest they should imagine it to be a self. (14)
Its cessation occurs at the stage of Arhatship.

However, the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) arises and functions from that very storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It ceases only when the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*) has become manifest and during the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). For one who has emerged from those two states, it functions again from the storehouse-consciousness alone. But at the stage of Arhatship, it ceases in every respect. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also arises and functions from the storehouse-consciousness at every moment.
It arises only except in the state of non-perception, in the attainment of non-perception, in the attainment of cessation, and during the two mindless states of torpor and fainting.

The remaining five consciousnesses arise from that very storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) according to conditions, either simultaneously or successively, like waves in a body of water, because the storehouse-consciousness alone is the substratum of all seeds. Such, then, is saṃsāra.

III.5.4.3.9 How is nirvāṇa? Here, through the power of cultivation, supramundane knowledge arises for yogins. Furthermore, for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, that [knowledge] has all phenomena as its object by way of the emptiness of the self-nature of the self; but for Bodhisattvas, it is also by way of the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper. Through the cultivation of that, the knowledge first arisen is called the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because of the seeing of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) not previously seen.

Then, that very same [object] when brought repeatedly before the mind is called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Through these two [paths], by the complete eradication of all latent afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*) to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation, one becomes a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha Arhat. However, when a Bodhisattva, according to the circumstances across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), effects the eradication of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of those abandoned afflictions as well as the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), he then becomes a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksambuddha.
For these three types of Arhats, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) ceases.

III.5.4.3.9.1 [A4r4] What is its transformation (*vyāvṛtti*)? It is the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). It is the cessation of the basis—characterized as the mental continuum—in its defiled aspect, while its pure aspect continues to function as long as space endures. Because at that time the latencies (*vāsanā*), which are the seeds of all defiled phenomena (*sāṃkleśika-dharma*), are completely eradicated, the state of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is characterized by being the support for those [seeds], is then abandoned. And due to the exhaustion of the seeds, no defiled phenomena arise.

And that basis at that time is called the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). Like space, it is of a single flavor. Because the seeds of the cognitions appearing as the environment, enjoyments, and bodies have been exhausted and do not arise again, it is also called the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*).

III.5.4.3.9.2 [A4r5] For this very reason, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not differ from the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas in terms of their *vimuktikāya* (body of liberation), because the *vimuktikāya* of all is indistinguishable, resembling pure crystal. They do, however, differ from them by way of the *dharmakāya*. For the *vimuktikāya* of all consists in the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) through the exhaustion of afflictions; whereas for the Perfectly Awakened Ones, that same [revolution] is also the *dharmakāya*, insofar as it is the body of the dharmas—that is, the basis of the Buddha-qualities.

What is their basis? It is due to the support of the power of their vows and the accumulation of immeasurable merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasambhāra*). Being distinguished by the *dharmakāya* itself, they are further distinguished from others by the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) comprised within the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. For example, the sun and moon are not distinguished from other waters, fires, or crystals merely by their purity; rather, they are distinguished as exceedingly great because of the empowerment of beings of great majesty and the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.

III.5.4.3.10 Now, what is the appearance of all phenomena within the supramundane gnosis of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas? It is of a single flavor with suchness, resembling the pure, infinite, and solitary sky. Why? Because therein all signs of the dharmic nature of all phenomena have set.

If, as you say, there were a single-form supramundane cognition regarding phenomena that possess diverse forms, it would be nothing but an error and not right knowledge. Therefore, names and signs are indeed unreal within all unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*). This is also stated in the *Aviparyāsaniveśana*:

"Indeed, Maitreya, this being so, that which is the object characterized by formative forces (*saṃskāra-nimitta*) is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*). Upon it, this adventitious designation has been superimposed, namely 'this is form,' up to 'these are the qualities of a Buddha. Furthermore, whether one abides in mere conceptual construction or in the non-conceptual realm (*nirvikalpa-dhātu*), when conceptual constructions arise, what existence or non-existence of it can be perceived, upon which this adventitious designation is superimposed, namely 'this is form,' up to 'these are the qualities of a Buddha'?"
For in this context, the unreality of names and signs is illuminated by the fact that they exist merely as conceptual constructions and are not perceived within the non-conceptual state.
It is indeed unreal because it is devoid of both a single and a manifold nature. As it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"Just as a form is seen in a mirror, devoid of being either one or many, yet it does not exist there."
Thus is the state of being among existing things. ||16||

For here, by the word "existence" (*bhāva*), the cause of existence is meant, because the determination of the distinction between individual characteristics depends upon the distinction between causes. Therefore, all phenomena are mind-only, consciousness-only, and manifestation-only. There is no external object to be grasped by representation, nor does representation possess an intrinsic nature that acts as a grasper. Both of these constitute the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of phenomena, because they are imagined through mental discourses. Wherein do they consist of being imagined?

Due to the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), there arises the unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) which possesses the aspect of an object even though no object exists. This unreal imagination is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of phenomena; it is an error, a perversion, and false cognition. For indeed, the aspect of the grasped (*grāhya-ākāra*) and the aspect of the grasper (*grāhaka-ākāra*) that appear therein are themselves entirely false. It is merely through the force of delusion and the force of mental disturbance that the unreal imagination manifests in such a way.

That form of his is unreal. What is real? It is mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*). For this very reason, that mental aspect (*ākāra*) is called the cause of delusion and the cause of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), because it is the objective support of delusion. It is also called the "cause of duality," because it resembles duality. All causes of conceptual proliferation cease within supramundane gnosis (*lokottara-jñāna*); therefore, that is called non-delusive and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). For this reason, that too is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); its perfection consists precisely in its non-delusiveness through the perfection of non-perversion (*aviparyāsa-pariniṣpatti*).

Suchness (*tathatā*), however, is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) by virtue of its perfection as being changeless; for its very perfection consists in its being immutable. Other [factors] are causes of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) because they are beginningless; others are causes of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) due to the repeated practice thereof. Therefore, it is only the imagination of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*) that is the dependent nature (*paratantra*), and not correct knowledge. In that regard, the relationship of cause and effect is denied among those imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-dharma*) which are the signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca-nimitta*), because they are false. It is not denied, however, among the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) whose essence is luminosity (*prakāśa*). As it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
The cessation of causes and conditions,
the negation of a [substantial] cause, and the establishment of mind-only— this I call non-arising. (17)
The venerable Nāgārjuna also stated all of this:
"For herein nothing whatsoever arises, nor does anything whatsoever cease."
Only conditions themselves arise and cease;
the great elements and so forth, as described, are subsumed within consciousness.
"That which was falsely conceptualized indeed vanishes within knowledge" (19).

Thus, that which was taught as the great elements and so forth is subsumed—that is, included—within consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is because, even though external great elements and so forth do not exist, a consciousness appearing as such arises for the foolish. However, within supramundane knowledge (*jñāna*), which is utterly non-erroneous, it goes to its cessation, because it is falsely conceptualized; for that which is unreal was previously imagined through delusion. This is the meaning of the second verse.

III.5.4.3.11 Therefore, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of the Yogācāras and the Mādhyamikas is the same. There is only this slight distinction: the Yogācāras maintain that phenomena (*dharmas*) lack existence insofar as they are apprehended by the ignorant, because that [apprehended form] is false; however, they do possess existence insofar as they consist of luminosity (*prakāśa*), due to the necessity of the relationship between cause and effect, and because error is impossible when there is awareness of their own intrinsic nature (*nijasvarūpa*). Thus say the Yogācāras.

The Mādhyamikas, however, maintain that because it is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and because it is not superimposed, even by means of a body of luminosity that serves as a cause for non-delusion, phenomena possess neither existence nor non-existence; for they consider that even the causal relationship and self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) present therein are subtle and cannot withstand analysis.

15 III.5.4.3.12 As for what is said by some— that just as luminosity is the nature (*prakṛti*) of phenomena, so too are forms such as blue— this is incorrect, because it is devoid of both scripture and tradition.

20 III.5.4.3.13 Furthermore, as for what some Mādhyamika says: "Just as mind and mental factors exist, so too external objects and self-reflexive awareness do not exist; all minds and mental factors are inherently deluded. However, the form-body (rūpakāya) of the Bodhisattva, like a wish-fulfilling gem, acts spontaneously for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings in every way."

Abiding [in this], they attain perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Nor is there a negation of these very minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); for just as the non-existence of all phenomena is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), so too at that time there is the cessation of all their minds and mental factors due to their absolute non-existence. Therefore, because they have attained conformity with the ultimate truth, the ultimate truth is realized by those minds and mental factors. All of this is established through scripture (*āgama*), treatises (*śāstra*), and the methods of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-naya*).
It has indeed emerged outside [the path]; therefore, this is a wrong path and must be avoided from afar.

III.5.4.3.14 5 Now, what is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)? It is the object within the sphere of ordinary beings (*bāla*). What is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)? It is the object within the sphere of the noble ones (*ārya*). Each of these two is threefold: (1) the conventional as designation (*prajñaptisaṃvṛti*), which is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is mere linguistic convention; and (2) the conventional as practice (*pratipattisaṃvṛti*), which is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is false cognition.

The conventional reality of manifestation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛti*) is the sign (*nimitta*) of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because by means of it the perfected nature is indicated. Here, ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it is the object of supreme knowledge (*parama-jñāna*). Ultimate reality as attainment (*prāpti-paramārtha*) is *nirvāṇa*, because it is the fruit of supreme knowledge. Ultimate reality as practice (*pratipatti-paramārtha*) is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), because its ultimate reality consists in this [knowledge]. As it is said in the Sūtra: "That mind is also no-mind; therein there is neither existence nor non-existence."
Thus [it is said].
What is its meaning? "Mind" is so called because its nature is luminosity; "non-mind" is so called because it lacks a grasping subject.

Therein, there is no existence by way of the characteristic of a grasper, nor is there non-existence by way of the characteristic of luminosity; this is its meaning. As for what was stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"When things are analyzed by the intellect..."
An intrinsic nature is not apprehended;
therefore, they are taught to be ineffable and devoid of intrinsic nature. ||20||
When analyzed by the intellect, however, there is neither the dependent nor the imagined; since the perfected nature does not exist as a real entity, how can it be conceptualized by the intellect?
There is no intrinsic nature, nor is there representation-only.
There is neither an object nor a storehouse-consciousness;
for these have been conceptualized by fools, those bad logicians who are like corpses.
Having transcended signs, objects, representations, and whatever is the outflow of the mind, my sons move about free from conceptual construction.

Thus [it is said]. What is its meaning? This is the meaning: "By means of cognition" refers to the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*). "Intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena (*dharma*), which is comprised of the two [natures]. "Those" refers to the phenomena. By this much, the non-existence of the imagined (*parikalpita*) has been stated.

And because it is imagined within this [dependent nature], for that very reason, when being analyzed by the intellect—that is, when being separated out as an object of apprehension—the dependent nature and even the perfected nature are non-existent due to their being imagined. How then could they be conceptualized or discerned by the intellect of yogins seeking the ultimate truth? They do not reach cessation; such is the meaning of the second verse. The two natures are the sign (nimitta) and representation (vijñapti). These two constitute the "entity" (vastu). The storehouse consciousness (ālaya) is the attachment (abhiniveśa) to what is being imagined; that too is the ultimate truth.

"Nothing exists at all; it is merely conceptualized by fools who are like corpses due to their lack of noble gnosis (*āryajñāna*), for these bad logicians do not transcend conceptual construction. This is the meaning of the third verse: the censure of those yogins who do not transcend conceptual construction.
For when analyzed by the intellect, there is neither the dependent nature nor the imagined;
since the perfected nature does not exist as a real entity, how can it be conceptualized by the intellect?
[LAS X.374] The meaning of the fourth verse concerns the praise of those who transcend these.
III.5.4.3.15 This much, in brief, is the Mahāyāna as it has been taught in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"The five dharmas, the [three] natures, and the eight consciousnesses."
The entirety of the Mahāyāna is comprised within two types of selflessness. ||24||

In this context, there are five factors: name (*nāman*), sign (*nimitta*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). Here, "name" refers to sound mounted upon mental discourse; "sign" refers to the object; "conceptualization" refers to the construction of the unreal (*abhūtaparikalpa*); "suchness" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); and "correct cognition" refers to supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*). Furthermore, the two forms of selflessness—personal selflessness (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomenal selflessness (*dharma-nairātmya*)—constitute the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding the state of things as they truly are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
III.5.5.1 It has been stated by the Blessed One that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature.
Thus it is said. How so? Because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form, up to and including the Buddha-qualities, which are empty of the intrinsic nature of Buddha-qualities.

Indeed, that essence of form which, through the mention of whichever entity, there arises in the world a cognition of form as "this is form" without distinction—that is the nature of form, namely *rūpatva*.

And that [object] is either a mere name or non-different from the name; it is a generality of form (*rūpasāmānya*). In this regard, that which is the name is not the form; thus, it is empty of that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the generality of form does not exist in itself, because momentariness is negated for anything non-momentary. That which is non-different from the name, however, does not exist at all; and since it is even more emphatically not the form, form is empty of that intrinsic nature. This applies likewise up to the Buddha-qualities.

Furthermore, if the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing were the object of speech and conceptual construction, then those two would not exist in the absence of the thing. Moreover, these two—namely, the false speech that "King Mahāsammata existed" and the false obsession that "Śaṅkha will be a universal monarch"—would not occur; nor would there be a difference of opinion, such as "sound is eternal" versus "sound is impermanent," because it is impossible for two contradictory intrinsic natures to be one at the same time. Therefore, because they lack an intrinsic nature characterized by the manifestation of a name, things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"By whatever name each and every phenomenon is expressed,"
"That [duality] does not exist therein; for that is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena.
The commentary on this is found in the *Triṃśikā*:
"By whichever conceptual construction..."
Whatever object is conceptualized, that is merely the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva); it does not exist. //26//
Moreover, it was said by the Blessed One: thus.

"Indeed, there is no form externally; it is one's own mind that appears as the external. (27) This triple world is mind-only. (28) And: "Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and representation (*vijñapti*) are synonyms. (29) Thus, since all phenomena have the nature of consciousness-only, they are devoid of intrinsic nature because they lack the nature of both the grasped object and the grasping subject.

Now, what is the reasoning here for the claim that these [phenomena] have consciousness alone as their intrinsic nature? It is said: Here, for those phenomena that are manifesting, manifestation is established by experience as their very essence. Manifestation means being made known, appearing, or shining forth. This indeed is a non-inert, immediate, and perfectly distinct form. If this were not established, then because nothing unmanifest could be established, there would follow the consequence of the non-establishment of everything. Since it is established, that itself is cognition; thus, all phenomena are established as having cognition as their intrinsic nature.

III.5.5.2.1 The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that luminosity is the object of the self's enjoyment; thus, it is established that this is a property of the object to be grasped, an effect of cognition, and not the essence of cognition itself.

That is incorrect; for it is precisely through the manifestation of blue and so forth as being experienced in their specific determinations—by means of which they are established as being experienced in those specific determinations—that this [manifestation] is established, and not otherwise.

Not even by a thousand causal factors [could this be established]. Therefore, because it is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) by virtue of being both the ultimate and the differentiator, this very [consciousness] is the cause and the causal factor (*kāraka*) in cognition. Consequently, it is logical that this alone is knowledge (*jñāna*), on the grounds that "it is known by means of this. Or else, that very cognition itself is knowledge, on the grounds that "knowledge is the act of knowing" (*jñāna-vijñāna*). In either case, all phenomena (*dharma*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, are established as having the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-rūpa*). For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of knowledge apart from that [consciousness], and because it is observed that [cognition] arises only when the causes of knowledge are present.

III.5.5.2.2 25 “O Sons of the Conqueror, the triple world is mind-only,” according to the Sūtra. Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and representation (*vijñapti*) are synonyms.

This illumination characterized as described above is not a property of either the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) or of the cognition (*jñāna*). Rather, it is solely the illumination of the external object, which is the arising of its cognition. As for the illumination of the cognition itself, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that it is simply the arising of that very cognition.

That is utterly inconsistent. For when objects exist, their luminous nature—which is established by experience—cannot be set aside even by Brahmā; and in their absence, cognitions of blue and so forth cannot be produced even by Śakra. Furthermore, even upon the arising of a cognition, blue and the like remain in an indistinct state, characterized by being beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*). The same applies to the cognition itself when that [second-order] cognition arises. Consequently, neither cognition nor the object would be manifest, and the world would become blind and mute.

But was it not said that cognition itself is the manifestation of the object? How can cognition, which is itself unmanifest, be the manifestation of something remote? If you say "because of its determination," how can something unmanifest be determined? If you say "it is manifested," then this very state of being manifested—that which is manifested as a clearly distinct form—is the manifestation; thus, how is it not a property of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)? And once the property of the object of knowledge is established, the rest is as explained before.
III.5.5.2.3 Knowledge, because its nature is luminosity,
manifests by itself; the object, however, is not of that nature.
Another [teacher] maintains that it manifests by virtue of its connection with cognition.

If it does not possess that form, then it does not manifest. To say that it is manifested yet does not manifest is a contradiction. Furthermore, on what basis is the object known by means of that [cognition]? If you argue that it is due to a connection consisting in their dependence upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*), then the eye itself would also be known by visual consciousness. If you argue that this is because the eye is not its object (*aviṣaya*), then what constitutes the "object-status" (*viṣayatā*) of a visible form (*rūpa*) when it lacks manifestation?
By this, the claim that "it is known because it is an object" is also refuted.
Another [teacher] holds that an object becomes manifest through contact with the illumination of cognition, just as a jar or similar object is manifested through contact with the light of a lamp.

Then its odors, tastes, and tangibles would also be cognized by visual consciousness, as would the color in fruits, flowers, and so forth, because there is no difference in their contact. If it is argued that this is not the case because they are not objects [of sight], the answer to this has already been stated. Therefore, everything blue and so on that is being experienced is cognition itself;
there is no external object distinct from cognition that serves as its apprehended referent. (32)

III.5.5.2.4 But the Sautrāntikas say: "This is acceptable to us; for us, all cognition is indeed endowed with an aspect (*sākāra*). However, that aspect is a reflection of the object, by means of which the object is directly impressed upon the mirror of cognition; that object is what is experienced by that cognition."

[Objection: Because there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the cognition of that [object] when there is the experience of its reflection, just like the experience of one’s own face on the surface of a mirror. [Reply: In that case, the manifestation of the object in the external mirror is erroneous due to a lack of extreme similarity; however, in the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*), it is non-erroneous because of extreme similarity. [Objection: Then from what kind of relationship does that cognition of the object by means of that cognition arise? If you say "from its arising [therefrom]," then the eye would also be cognized by visual consciousness. If you say "from similarity of form" (*sārūpyāt*), [then...]

If this is argued, then it would follow that many people perceiving the same object would experience one another’s cognitions. If it is argued that [cognition is the object] because of its arising from it and its similarity to it, then the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)—being of a similar nature—would also become the object. Furthermore, if there were similarity in every respect, cognition would partake of the nature of non-cognition. If there were similarity in some respect, then everything would be the cognition of everything.
For if there were similarity in every respect, cognition would indeed become non-cognition.
If there were identity in some respect, everything would be a cognizer of everything.
Nor does a corresponding cognition arise from an object, because this is subject to deviation, as seen in the case of a horse in a dream; therefore, an apprehended object does not exist at all.

If it is asked how cognition can have the form of an object when no object exists, and how there can be a restriction by place and time: [the answer is that] even in the absence of an object, cognition arises with the appearance of an object restricted by place and time from the mind, which is afflicted by the latencies of beginningless conceptual construction, just as in a dream when one is afflicted by drowsiness.
And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"An external object does not exist in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish; rather, the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as an object.

Moreover, this entire universe consisting of the eighteen elements is not one, due to the differentiation of the elements. Even the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is not one, due to the differentiation of bodies, houses, trees, and so forth. Even the body is not one. "Ruṭhitam" means struck or afflicted; for according to the root-dictionary (*dhātupāṭha*), the roots *ruṭh* and *luṭh* signify affliction (*upaghāta*). (35)

If it is asked how there can be a commonality of error among many people in one place, it is due to the commonality of the impairment. It is like the commonality of errors regarding hair, mosquitoes, and so forth, among many people when there is a common impairment of the eyes by cataracts (*timiropaghāta*). However, occasional correspondence occurs due to the firmness of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), as in the case of a dream of horses. Therefore, since there is nothing whatsoever that is an object of apprehension (*grāhya*), there is also nothing whatsoever that is an apprehending subject (*grāhaka*). Consequently, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), empty of both apprehended object and apprehending subject.

[It is not one] because of the distinctions between the hand, the foot, and so forth. The hand, too, is not one because of the distinctions between the index finger and the others. The index finger, too, is not one because of the distinctions between its joints. A joint, too, is not one because of the distinctions between its parts. Even a part of a joint and so forth is not one, as it possesses constituent parts due to the distinctions between those parts.

If it is argued that a single atom must be partless, we reply: no, for a single atom is never perceived, since there is only the appearance of something gross and solid. If it is argued that many atoms appear in that way when conjoined, [we respond]: if atoms are partless, they cannot have conjunction by means of a part. If, on the other hand, conjunction occurs through their entirety, then because all of them would occupy the same location, the entire terrestrial sphere would be no larger than a single atom.

And everything else belonging to the category of form that is conjoined with earth appears [as such]; therefore, both that [other form] and earth—all this would appear as a mere single atom. But it is not so. Therefore, there is here neither a single atom nor anything else. In the absence of things of a single form, that which consists of their collection—

There is no such thing [as a single atom]. Therefore, the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is neither one nor many. Furthermore, there is no other mode of existence for a real entity (*vastu*) apart from unity and plurality. Consequently, this realm of form is purely false and not a real entity. And just as it is with the realm of form, so it is with the realms of sound, odor, taste, and tangibles, as well as the realms of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, because these too are merely aggregates of atoms.

Thus, because the five objects and the five bases do not exist, the five consciousness-elements—eye-consciousness and the rest—are non-existent. Due to their non-existence, the mental-consciousness-element also does not exist; for in that case, one should simply say "consciousness," and not "mental-consciousness," since the qualification would be redundant.

The mind-element (*manodhātu*) also does not exist. For it is held that the mind-element is precisely that which among the six consciousnesses has just passed away, because it serves as the basis for the subsequent consciousness. Since this [mind-element] exists apart from the six [consciousnesses], it is merely a conceptual designation (*prājñaptika*) and not substantially real (*dravyasat*). Furthermore, because it is not distinct from the six consciousnesses, it does not exist even by way of negating those six;
therefore, the mind-element also does not exist. And due to its absence, the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) also does not exist.

The *dharmadhātu* remains. And what is it? It consists of external form (the ten bases), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). [Objection: Is it not the case that form does not exist at all, just as in the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), because it is merely an aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*)? If you argue that non-informative form (*avijñapti*) is not an aggregation of atoms, then why is it not accepted as being formless (*arūpin*)? Furthermore, non-informative form has been refuted by the Teachers (*ācārya*). Mental factors are those which exist in the mind; "mind," "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are synonyms.

And thus, from the negation of the six consciousnesses, there follows the negation of the mental factors (*caitasika*). Furthermore, these mental factors are taught as having a basis and an object that are not distinct from the mind; therefore, they are also negated by the negation of the six bases (*āśraya*), and likewise by the negation of the six objects (*ālambana*)—both those already established and those yet to be established. The formations dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) are [negated] from among other formations according to their respective applications. And the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*) because it lacks a distinct nature or body separate from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, even the dharma-element does not exist at all. Because of its absence, and because of the negation of the object of perception, the mental-consciousness-element also does not exist.
Therefore, the eighteen elements do not exist. By the negation of the elements, the negation of the sense-bases and the aggregates is established.
"Just as a form in a mirror is seen devoid of both identity and difference, yet it does not exist [as that form], so too is the nature of things among entities.

(36) And this very aspect of cognition, such as blue and so forth, is indeed false and not a real entity; for even if it were of the nature of cognition, the persistence of its lack of both unity and plurality remains unchanged. It is stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*)—
And because by the mention of "that" (tat), it is stated that [the object] is the cause of the error produced by the impairment [of the senses].
Just as a form is seen in a mirror, devoid of both identity and difference, yet it does not exist [as that which is seen], so too is the characteristic of arising. [LAS X.709] III.5.5.3.1

How, then, can there be the appearance of those [objects], such as the aggregates (*skandha*), when they do not exist? Even though they do not exist, that appearance arises from the mind itself, due to the affliction of its latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), just as before. And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:

How does this unreal [object] appear? It appears precisely by means of its nature as manifestation (*prakāśātmatva*), which is itself unreal. For consciousness alone, being manifest due to its nature as manifestation, is erroneous because it is afflicted by the turbulence of beginningless habitual tendencies of delusion (*bhrānti-vāsanā*). It appears through unreal forms such as blue and so forth, just as in dreams and the like, because the manifestation of blue and so forth is established; for that [manifestation] would be impossible without the nature of manifestation. Furthermore, even though blue and so forth are manifesting, their unreality is established by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*);
and once that is established, the unreality of their identity with [consciousness] is also established.

The establishment of luminosity as a real entity, however, follows from the fact that its cognition is not subject to error, because it is a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For luminosity has luminosity itself as its innate nature; thus, it cannot be brought about by a cognitive distortion (*viplava*), such that the cognition of it would be erroneous. Blue, on the other hand, being a different form, may indeed be brought about by a distortion, and thus the cognition of it could be erroneous. Consequently, while there is scope for a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*) regarding blue and the like, there is none regarding luminosity.

III.5.5.3.2 Some Yogācāras and some Mādhyamikas who maintain that cognition possesses an aspect (sākārajñānavādins) say this: "The identity between the blue object and its manifestation is impossible because they are endowed with contradictory properties—the one being unreal and the other real. And if there were no identity, the blue would not manifest. Therefore, the blue is the very self of the manifestation. Furthermore, the blue is either a real entity or non-superimposed; for it is non-different from a manifestation that is either a real entity or non-superimposed."

Since they would perceive their own nature without error through all those very manifestations, there would be an absolute absence of delusion. Consequently, all sentient beings would be eternally liberated and eternally perfectly awakened. (37) If it is argued that conceptual cognition is a delusion because it determines an object in its own manifestation despite the object not being present, [we ask: how is it that the object being determined by it is not manifested? Or, if it is being manifested, how is it that it does not appear within that [cognition]? A—

If it were to manifest [as the object], then there would be the consequence of its identity with that object; furthermore, if the object were non-existent, that manifestation would not occur. Moreover, there would be certainty in every respect regarding such cases as "Māndhātṛ existed," "Śaṅkha will exist," "the self exists," and "sound is eternal. It would also manifest through its own distinct characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as "cow"; and since the application of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is impossible with respect to a particular characteristic, that cognition would not be conceptual (*vikalpikā*) at all.

Therefore, it must be accepted that the cognition of a cow appears through a distortion (*viplava*) in the form of a false, verbalized [concept]—namely, "cowness" (*gotva*), which is common to all individual cows without exception—and that this appearance constitutes the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object "cow. For in this way, these faults would not arise; for even though the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not appear [in the cognition], it is determined through error (*bhrānti*). Indeed, error is a distortion of the intellect. In that regard, there is an identity (*tādātmya*) between both [the particular and the universal] in the case of "cowness," which is characterized by the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*).
And because of identity, there is appearance and conceptual determination; all this is a distortion of the intellect and not the reality of things, and therefore it is not to be refuted.

For those whose intellects are deluded, things are established according to their appearance rather than according to reality; this is because such appearance is established by experience, is an indispensable factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and is thus difficult to deny, yet it cannot be [said to be] according to reality. This is because when there is a determination (*adhyavasita*) regarding the mere exclusion of the non-cow, and when [the cognition] is restricted to that alone, correspondence (*saṃvāda*) is possible. Furthermore, just as the unreal "cowness" (*gotva*) appears in the cognition of a cow and possesses identity (*tādātmya*) with it, its being a real entity or its being non-superimposed does not follow from its non-difference [from the cognition].

Likewise, in the manifestation of blue and so forth, the establishment of identity between the blue and its manifestation is indeed established, because there is no contradiction between unreality and reality when they reside in different forms within even a single entity. Furthermore, if "identity" alone were the reason (*hetu*) for proving either substantiality or non-superimposition, then it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the presence of] cowness (*gotva*) and the like. If, however, "non-superimposed identity" were the reason, that is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Therefore, this remains settled: all these phenomena are mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*), devoid of grasped object and grasping subject.
III.5.5.4 In that regard, those phenomena belonging to the three realms which, despite the absence of duality, appear as dual, are—

Unreal imagination [is the basis]. The duality of the grasped and the grasper, imagined by mental discursive thoughts according to its appearance, is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). The emptiness of that [unreal imagination] with respect to that very duality is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

And that emptiness of duality is not a non-entity, because its characteristic is the absence of duality; nor is it an absolute non-existence, because this absence of duality is precisely the existence of representation-only (vijñaptimātra), which is empty of duality. It is not a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), for a non-implicative negation is in no way an entity, whereas [in our case] there is an entity because it follows the nature of an implicative negation (*paryudāsa*), and "it exists" is an entity. Therefore, in reality, that [non-existence] does not exist; it is merely imagined. But from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is indeed an implicative negation as described.

And since that [emptiness] is the very *dharmatā* of the unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), it is therefore neither different from it nor non-different from it, because of the difference in their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For that which is the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena is not itself [identical to] the phenomenon due to its uniqueness. This is one way in which there is a difference of characteristics. Furthermore, specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are defined by the delineation of signs (*nimitta-ullekha*). [Emptiness is] void—

That [emptiness] is, however, by means of the setting of all signs; this is the second distinction of its characteristic. And because it is merely the emptiness of duality, undifferentiated according to its characteristic at all times in all phenomena, it is said to be eternal, pervasive, and changeless. Since the stains of names and signs are unreal, and since the stains of obscuration are contingent upon signs, those adventitious stains do not constitute its essence. Furthermore, the nature of phenomena is their *dharmatā*.
But since the stains arise from adherence to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), they are removed through the removal of that [adherence]; thus, they too are adventitious to it.

Whatever is meditated upon becomes clearly manifest when the culmination of that meditation is reached, as in the case of a beloved woman appearing within a continuous stream of desire, grief, fear, and so forth. Furthermore, the four stages of yoga (*yogabhūmi*)—the limited nature of phenomena, mind-only, emptiness with signs, and signlessness—are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and these are what are meditated upon.

Regarding that, the Yogācāras maintain that on the fourth stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*), there is supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*) which has the emptiness of all phenomena as its object, is entirely without appearance, and is like the pure, infinite sky. The Mādhyamikas agree with this. For it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"The great elements and so forth, as they are taught, are subsumed within consciousness."
Indeed, that which is falsely conceptualized vanishes upon the arising of knowledge.
(38) Thus it is said.

However, there is this distinction: the Yogācāras maintain that which is the mere luminosity (*prakāśamātra*), the intrinsic nature of phenomena, exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*); whereas the Mādhyamikas maintain that even that does not exist substantially. This is a rootless quarrel between the Mādhyamikas and the Yogācāras; thus, one might utter a verse in reproach of such common folk:
