"Those for whom all conduct is identical when reality is not seen, yet whose knowledge is likewise one and the same—free from darkness—once reality is seen; alas, what a kinship there is among kinsmen with the Yogācāras!"
Why, then, do they engage in this quarrel with those who are beloved by the mediators?

In this regard, those Mādhyamikas who advocate for external objects and those who advocate for cognition with forms (*sākāra-jñāna*) have already been refuted by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), as they fall outside the scope of both scripture and treatise. Only those who advocate for representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) without forms (*nirākāra*) remain. For them as well, how can manifestation (*prakāśa*) be unreal? If it is argued that it is so because it is not distinct from the unreal—just like the forms of blue and so forth—that is not the case; for the non-distinctness of that which is not superimposed is unestablished (*asiddha*). Mere non-distinctness is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the contrary instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

For it is possible for an identity (*tādātmya*) to be superimposed upon that which is not so [in reality] by means of that which is so, just as in the case of the cognitions of "cowness," "permanence," and so forth. Alternatively, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikānta*) due to the deviation caused by emptiness (*śūnyatā*). If it is argued that emptiness itself is false, then the vision of emptiness would also be an error, like the vision of blue and other such objects; and a form superimposed by error is indeed false. However, luminosity (*prakāśa*), being the innate nature of luminosity, is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because it is partless.
Furthermore, this is the innate nature of all entities (*bhāva*), since it is established for both [parties] by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore...
That which is falsely conceptualized indeed vanishes upon the arising of knowledge.
This [reality], being established in its own nature, is proven to be non-superimposed and non-illusory. "Illusory," "unreal," and "superimposed by delusion" are synonyms.

If it is argued that "non-existence" refers simply to the absence of another property (dharma) characterized by existence, and that we call this very thing "unreal" rather than "superimposed," even so, the reason remains unestablished and inconclusive, as before. Furthermore, if the subverting argument (bādhaka) establishes only non-existence and not superimposition, then the form of those cognitions which are subverted would be their own intrinsic nature; thus, there would be no error at all. And the fault in that case has already been stated:
"In that [cognition], that which was falsely conceptualized surely vanishes. (39)

Thus, this [position] is contradicted. Therefore, it is established that the non-existence of that which is being perceived is pervaded by its being superimposed. Consequently, through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), there is a negation of the non-existence of manifestation; therefore, its existence is established. Furthermore, an uncontradicted form and an uncontradicted perception constitute existence, and both of these are established for manifestation; thus, its existence cannot be denied. In the case of blue and so forth, however, both are contradicted because their status as superimpositions is established by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*); therefore, their non-existence is logical.

Furthermore, what else do you wish to negate regarding the existence of luminosity? If you say it is its being dependently originated and its causal efficacy (*arthakriyāśakti*), then what is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for these two? If you say it is the absence of being either one or many, [we reply: does this not directly subvert the very nature of the entity and [only] imply the subversion of its power? Since the nature of luminosity is itself unsubvertible, its power must likewise be unsubvertible. Indeed, it is not merely the form of blue and so forth that is subverted, because they are manifest; rather, it is the nature of the real entity (*vasturūpa*) [that would be subverted].

If it is argued that what is sublated is indeed that very capacity (*śakti*), then, in that case, since there would be no distinction between the blue object and its manifestation, the theory of "cognition with form" (*sākāravāda*) would follow; and that has already been refuted previously. [Indeed, that which is falsely conceptualized ceases upon the knowledge of that reality. (YṢ 34cd)

Therefore, this absence of being one or many would apply only to that [form] which is superimposed, because it is established according to how it is perceived, and not to that which is non-superimposed, because it is established according to its true nature. Consequently, by this [reasoning], the superimposed form is directly sublated, but the capacity (*śakti*) is not. Thus, the very establishment of the blue and other forms as being superimposed constitutes their sublation; since that [superimposition] is impossible for luminosity (*prakāśa*), there is no sublation of luminosity. Therefore, the negation of capacity pertains to the object such as blue, and not to luminosity.

"In that case, these two—namely, [the arguments] that [an effect] arises from a potency and that it arises from what has perished—are subverting proofs, because that which has perished and that which has not perished lack causal efficacy, since there is no production of either the existent or the non-existent. These two, too, are not subverting proofs, because they are unestablished (*asiddha*). For there is no contradiction in a cause that has not perished producing its effect immediately thereafter; and there is no contradiction in an effect being produced from a cause in which it was previously non-existent.

Moreover, from what is the absence of both causal capacity (*śakti*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpannatva*) ascertained? For perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not determinative because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*), nor is mere conceptualization (*vikalpamātra*) sufficient, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that a determination (*avasāya*)—whether born of perception or born of a logical mark (*liṅga*)—is determinative of its own cause, the object, due to a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), then [that cause] must already be established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For how could that causal relationship (hetuphalabhāva) be subverted? And if the causal relationship were unestablished, there would be no directed engagement with or withdrawal from specific objects for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful. If it is argued: "The causal relationship is indeed established, but only conventionally (saṃvṛtyā) and not ultimately (paramārthataḥ), because the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of phenomena cannot withstand analysis," [we reply: But if efficacy (śakti) is established by valid cognition (pramāṇa), how can it be incapable of withstanding analysis? If you say: "Because the proving and refuting cognitions possess equal force," [we respond:]...

For this very reason, let there be a distinction: blue and so forth are conventionally real because, although they are perceived, they are sublated; however, consciousness, whose very body is light, has the manifestation of blue and so forth as its nature, and it is ultimately real because it cannot be sublated and because it possesses powers established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, you consider the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena to be unsublatable because it is perceived; in that case, power (*śakti*) is all the more unsublatable, since it is established by valid cognition.

Therefore, if the existence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) were established for phenomena, their very lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) would be subverted. Consequently, the subversion of the essential form of blue and other objects—which is characterized by the establishment of their being superimposed—occurs directly through the subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). By implication, the establishment of [their] impossibility and so forth follows; it is not the case that the manifestation itself is superimposed. Thus, the Yogācāra position is difficult to refute: manifestation is either ultimately real (*paramārtha-sat*) or conventionally real (*saṃvṛti-sat*), but it cannot be both.

"Because it is not superimposed, or because of the absence of superimposition, it is like emptiness"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively, there is either the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) or the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). If luminosity were indeed substantially existent, then why was it stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"O Mahāmati, all phenomena are unarisen, because of the non-arising of both the existent and the non-existent"?

What is the meaning of this? Restriction is understood therein: that which is eternally existent as the *dharmadhātu*, and that which is eternally non-existent as the imagined object (*parikalpita-artha*). Because these two do not arise, they are "unproduced," but not even the nature of cognition (*jñāna-ātman*) is unproduced; such is its meaning. For this very reason, it is said there:
"The cessation of causes and conditions, the negation of a [substantial] cause, and the establishment of Mind-only—I declare this to be 'non-arising' (anutpāda). (40)

Thus, the meaning of the verse is that the negation of [the status of] cause, condition, and causal factor apart from mind, and the establishment [of everything] within mind-only, is non-arising (*anutpāda*). This was also stated by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"No phenomenon whatsoever arises, nor does anything whatsoever cease."
"Only conditions arise and cease. As for what was then stated in the *Ārya-śālistamba* and other texts:
Therefore, this [world] is not uncreated, nor self-created, nor created by another, nor created by both, nor is it arisen without a cause.

What is the meaning of this? This is its meaning: it is not created by a mere cause, nor by a mere condition, nor by both, because of the absence of action (*kriyā*), effort (*samīhā*), and agency (*kartṛtva*). For no action is perceived in anything, nor is it logically tenable, because all things are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary; how can there be activity for those that are unstable? Their very arising is what constitutes activity, and that itself is called the agent" (43).

Nor is there any volition (*samīhā*), for it does not occur to a seed, "I shall produce a sprout. Nor is there agency (*kartṛtva*), for entities are dependent upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); among them, who could be independent enough to be an agent? However, it is not even the mere relationship between cause and effect that is denied here.
Nor is it produced without a cause, according to the statement [of the Buddha]. For this very reason, he says later:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."

For in this context, by stating that the production of the effect occurs immediately after the continuum of the cause, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and the three types of perception and non-perception that establish it have been stated. By the restriction "only when [the cause exists]," which states that the effect is not produced when the cause ceases, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and the two types of non-perception that establish it have been stated. By this much alone, the agency and effort (*kriyā-samīhā*) are implicitly negated. Furthermore, by the phrase "from the arising of this," the negation of agency is established because that which is being produced is dependent upon causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pāratantryāt*).

Thus, when the causal relationship between two continua has been established in a general sense, its establishment regarding specific instances also follows from the two types of observation. Indeed, those same two observations, due to the distinction of their objects, constitute three instances of perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*). If it is asked how multiple momentary and non-conceptual perceptions can determine a causal relationship, [the answer is]:
by means of the very final [perception] which arises through the power of the certainty of preceding experiences, as it is precisely that which directly determines it according to the circumstances.

III.5.5.4.1.1 10. As for that which some Mādhyamika says: "Conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is worldly consensus; and according to worldly consensus, there is an external object"—even that exists conventionally, like mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). However, mind and mental factors are erroneous, because from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), self-cognition is a contradiction—like a sword cutting itself—and because cognition of another is merely a delusion, as agreed upon by both [parties].

Therefore, the destruction of delusion and the ultimate perfect awakening (*paramārthasambodha*) of the Buddhas consist precisely in the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*). For when these [factors] are absolutely non-existent for them, then the absolute non-existence of all phenomena (*dharmāṇām atyantābhāvaḥ*), which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), becomes known to them through the attainment of conformity with it. However, non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhitanirodha*) occurs because, after the ultimate perfect awakening, they maintain a form-body (*rūpakāya*) in order to accomplish the welfare of the world.

That is more evil than evil. For in that case, since it is the absence of mind and mental factors, it lacks form and is therefore not cognition; how then could that itself be the ultimate awakening? Now—

At that time, cognition is indeed nothing but mind, and that mind does not exist without mental factors (*caitta*); so how could there be an absence of both mind and mental factors? Furthermore, if there were a perception of an ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) as something distinct [from consciousness], it would follow that it is an error. If it were non-distinct, it would follow that it is self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). Moreover, if "non-existence" means nothing at all, then there is neither an ultimate reality nor a perception of an ultimate reality. Furthermore, the ultimate reality is the absolute non-arising of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), and that is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

The non-arising after a long period of having arisen, according to conventional reality, belongs only to certain minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*). From what, then, does their similarity [to the Buddha] derive? If it is argued that they are similar merely in their non-arising, then since the non-arising of all destroyed or unarisen minds and mental factors exists eternally for everyone, all sentient beings would possess ultimate awakening at all times. But this is not the case. Therefore, the cessation of mind and mental factors is not ultimate awakening.

Furthermore, if all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are erroneous, what then is their antidote? If it is argued that error itself is the adversary when it is gross, while it is the antidote when it is subtle, then the final error would be without an antidote; thus, there would be no absence of minds and mental factors.

Moreover, being manifest (*saṃvedyatā*) is nothing other than immediacy (*aparokṣatā*). And this cannot exist without a connection with luminosity (*prakāśa*). Luminosity is simply the nature of clarity; its connection with that nature is indeed identity (*tādātmya*). Since that which cannot be known without something else must be known by means of that very thing, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is free from contradiction. Furthermore, since whatever is known is itself cognition (*jñāna*), it follows that the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*), being of the nature of cognition, are themselves self-aware.

Furthermore, since the relationship with luminosity is nothing other than identity (*tādātmya*), the state of "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātratā*) is established. Therefore, it is proven that there is no external object whatsoever to be grasped by consciousness. Because of the absence of such objects, the claim that non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*) is based upon the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is untenable. For this reason as well, perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) is not the non-existence of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

20. Now it is said: just as a sword-blade does not cut itself, and just as the tip of a finger does not touch itself, so too the mind does not see itself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. Therefore, there is no self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). As it is stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"Just as a sword does not cut its own blade, and just as a fingertip does not touch itself, so the mind does not see itself. (45)

Thus [it is said]. To this we reply: by this verse, the relationship of grasped and grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-bhāva*) is negated with respect to the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) of the mind, because that [relationship] is dependent upon duality, like the contact of cutting. However, self-cognition itself is not negated, because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*). For self-cognition is indeed manifestation (*prakhyāna*). Thus, since it is contradictory in the case of duality, it is restricted to non-duality; it is not negated. For this very reason, in the passage "so the mind sees itself," the ellipsis is "it does not grasp itself.
And as it is said in the *Āryasaṃdhinirmocana*:
Maitreya said: "Blessed One, if that reflected image within that range is other than that mind, how can that very mind observe that very same mind?
The Blessed One replied: "Maitreya, it is not that some phenomenon there observes some phenomenon; rather, that mind has arisen in such a way that it appears as such."

Thus it is said. Furthermore, within the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), the perception of cognition’s own intrinsic nature is the direct means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) because it is non-erroneous. However, the perception of superposed forms is an error. Therefore, having completely and gradually abandoned those very causes of error, that which is the perception of the emptiness of duality—the body of light of all phenomena, which resembles the pure, infinite sky—is [the ultimate realization].

Thus, it is not tenable that there is an extinction of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) through the realization of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sambodha*). Furthermore, because the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*), which are of the nature of consciousness, possess the power to project a continuous stream (*saṃtāna-avedha*), they are inexhaustible; for this reason as well, the extinction of the mind and mental factors is not tenable. Moreover, the basis (*āśraya*) characterized by the stream of mind and mental factors is called the *ālayavijñāna* as long as the seeds of the *sāsrava* (contaminated) phenomena have not been extinguished. When those [seeds] are extinguished, it is called the uncontaminated realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*), and the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*).
For this reason too, the extinction of the mind and mental factors is not tenable. And it was said by the Blessed One:

"The destruction of form is the impermanence of form, up to the destruction of consciousness is the impermanence of consciousness"—this is a counterfeit *prajñāpāramitā*. Therefore, the cessation of mind and mental factors is not logically tenable as enlightenment (*sambodha*). Furthermore, if non-erroneous supramundane gnosis were not accepted on the stages such as the Joyful (*pramuditā*) and so forth, then the jewel of the Dharma called *prajñāpāramitā*, the Sangha of Bodhisattvas, and the jewel of the Buddha would all be rejected.

But if [this] is accepted, the cessation of mind and mental factors as enlightenment is not logical. This same fault applies even to those who reject the non-manifesting *prajñāpāramitā*. The yogi remains established in the non-manifesting.
For manifestation (*prakāśa*) is indeed the clear form; through connection with that, there is immediacy (*aparokṣatā*).

That very [immediacy] is knowability (*vedyatā*), because of which, for whatever [object], consciousness belongs to it by virtue of that [connection]. It is like the tip of a finger and the edge of a sword.
The grasping at [the reality of] one's own [mental] constructs is warded off by the intellect;
it is clearly stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* that there is no self-manifestation (*svataḥkhyāti*). (2)
Therefore, self-cognition is established;
therefore, it is the defining characteristic of cognition.
(Perhaps this reflects the perspective of the Sautrāntikas: "the body is reduced to ashes and consciousness is extinguished.")
"He perceives the Mahāyāna," and so forth; thus, enough with this excessive detail. Here are the verses:
"And identity with the luminosity..."
From that, through yoga, there arises the state of pure intellect. || 3 ||
Knowledge of one's own nature is direct perception; regarding unreal things, there are only appearances and delusions.
Abandoning those, cultivate the Infinite.
Knowledge is like the sky, absolute.

The mental continuum is imperishable as long as the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has not been exhausted; when the seeds of tainted phenomena (sāsravadharma) are exhausted, it is the untainted realm (anāsravadhātu). || 5 ||
When [the obscurations] are exhausted, this is the body of liberation (vimuktikāya) and also the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) of the Protector;
it is the basis of the Buddha-qualities, just as the sun is the constant source of its rays.
Regarding the state of being as it truly is, there is the wisdom consisting of reflection.

III.6. The wisdoms consisting of hearing and reflection have been explained. It was previously stated that, having relied upon them, one should cultivate the perfection of wisdom; therefore, its cultivation must now be discussed. Furthermore, the application of hearing, reflection, and cultivation is twofold: devoted application (*satkṛtya-prayoga*) and continuous application (*sātatyaprayoga*). Application is activity. Application performed with care, affection, and reverence is devoted application. Uninterrupted application is continuous application.

III.6.1 Cultivation is threefold: calm abiding (*śamatha*), insight (*vipaśyanā*), and both calm abiding and insight. Among these, the non-conceptual image, the full extent of existence (*yāvadbhāvikatā*), and the mode of existence (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*) are the objects of calm abiding. The conceptual image, the full extent of existence, and the mode of existence are the objects of insight.

In this case, when a bodhisattva is alone and in seclusion, having brought to mind the objects as they were intended, and repeatedly attending to the very mind that reflects those objects while avoiding mental chatter—until physical pliancy and mental pliancy have arisen—that is attention conducive to calm abiding (*śamatha*). When these arise, then calm abiding is attained.

Having attained that pliancy of body and mind, and relying upon it, as he examines and gains conviction in those very objects as they were intended within the internal images that are the domain of meditative concentration, there is mental attention conducive to insight (vipaśyanā) for as long as pliancy of body and pliancy of mind have not yet arisen; when these arise, then there is insight.

Thereafter, when a continuous and uninterrupted flow of mental attention occurs toward both—the conceptual images themselves and that very mind which takes them as its object—then there are calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). At that time, it is called the path that proceeds with the two joined together (*yuganaddhavāhī*), because calm abiding and insight proceed like a pair, bound together in equilibrium.

There are five hindrances. Among them, restlessness and remorse are an obstruction to serenity (*śamatha*); lethargy, drowsiness, and doubt are obstructions to insight (*vipaśyanā*); sensual desire and ill-will are obstructions to both. When lethargy and drowsiness are well-composed, then serenity becomes purified. When restlessness and remorse are thoroughly subdued, then insight becomes purified.
In that regard, the ninefold *śamatha* has been taught by the Blessed One:
namely, he places the mind internally, settles it, stabilizes it, draws it near, tames it, pacifies it, completely tranquilizes it, makes it one-pointed, and concentrates the mind. (49)

In that regard, *sthāpanā* (placement) is the initial binding of the mind within for the sake of internal condensation, having withdrawn it from external objects. Following that, *saṃsthāpanā* (continuous placement) is the stabilization of that naturally mobile mind in that very continuity. Then, *avasthāpanā* (re-placement) is the withdrawal and re-binding of the mind after realizing it has been distracted outwardly due to a lapse of mindfulness.

Then, there is the further condensation and refinement of that which is by nature gross, as well as its repeated stabilization. Then, because one perceives the excellence of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is delighting in it and its mastery. Then, because one perceives the fault in distraction—the lack of delight in the state of elevation (*unnati*) due to such elevation—there is pacification, which is the calming [of the mind].

The pacification (*vyupaśamana*) of covetousness, dejection, and so forth that have arisen is their complete subsiding. Thereupon, because the mind flows spontaneously toward a single object, its activity becomes one-pointed (*ekoti*). The making one-pointed (*ekotīkaraṇa*) is the bringing about of such a state through effort for that which was not previously so. In that regard, through the practice of making one-pointed, there is right application (*samyaṅ-āya*) by way of effortless spontaneous flow, and the long-term maintenance (*āyata-dhāraṇa*) is concentration (*samādhāna*).
For it is said in the *Sūtrālaṃkāra*: "Having bound the mind to the object..."
One should not allow that which is bound to it to be distracted;
having quickly recognized distraction, one should again withdraw [the mind] back into that [object], concentrating it within. (50) In brief, [this is] regarding the internal.
The wise person should direct the mind higher and higher;
then, by perceiving its virtues, he should delight the mind in meditative concentration. ||51||

By seeing the fault in distraction, one should pacify covetousness, dejection, and so forth as they arise. (52) Then, through that practice, the practitioner shall again attain a state of spontaneous flow in the mind, which was previously accompanied by volitional effort, and subsequently attain a state free from volitional effort.
(53) Thus it has been said.
Vipaśyanā is also said to be fourfold; namely:
the discernment of phenomena, thorough discernment, complete investigation, and complete analysis.

"In that regard, the discernment (*vicaya*) of things as they exist in their full extent (*yāvadbhāvikānām*) is investigation (*pravicaya*). The discernment of things as they exist in their true nature (*yathāvadbhāvikānām*) is thorough analysis (*parivitarka*). The grasping of signs (*nimittākāropādāna*) by means of non-conceptual mental attention (*nirvikalpena manasikāreṇa*) accompanied by wisdom (*prajñāsahagatena*) is examination (*saṃtīraṇā*), which is thorough deliberation (*parimīmāṃsā*). (54) Their explanation is stated by the noble Maitreya in the *Mahāyānābhidharmasamuccaya*.

"What is insight (*vipaśyanā*)? It is as follows: that which discriminates phenomena, thoroughly discriminates them, reflects upon them, and engages in thorough investigation; doing so by means of the antidote to the signs of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*), and by means of the mental engagement that negates error and is non-erroneous. (55) 10

<The meaning of those terms here is as follows>: <Dauṣṭhulya is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of error>. <And that [impression] is characterized by its dependence upon the mental continuum (*cittasaṃtāna*), having the power to produce an intensification of error>. <Its signs are those things which nourish it, being preceded by successive instances of adherence to error>. <Through their destruction, because of the destruction of *dauṣṭhulya*, error no longer arises. The destruction of the sign occurs through the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the sign>.
<For the antidote is analytical investigation (*vicaya*), and it investigates thoroughly>.
Therefore, these two were taught by taking into account the antidote to the cause of corruption. 10.

"Thorough investigation is taught for the purpose of destroying error. Because he investigates correctly and discerns correctly, he thoroughly searches with non-discursive mental attention by means of the absolute elimination of the suspicion of error; therefore, it is called 'the destruction of error. In that way, it destroys error by making it non-erroneous."

"Investigation" (*parimīmāṃsā*) means that, having brought to mind an object directly perceived within that non-erroneous state, one observes it. Therefore, the meaning is that [this teaching] was taught based upon mental attention that is free from error. Likewise, through the perfection of the cultivation of the fourfold insight (*vipaśyanā*), one is liberated from the bondage of *dauṣṭhulya* (inner corruption) by virtue of that perfection. Through the perfection of the ninefold cultivation of tranquility (*śamatha*), one is liberated from the bondage of signs (*nimitta*), because [those signs] are characterized by the cessation of the objects of error and the errors themselves.
As it has been said:
"A living being is bound by the bond of signs and also by the bond of depravity; by cultivating insight and tranquility, one is liberated. (56) Thus it is said.

One should apply the meaning of that verse according to its logical fitness, and not merely according to the order of the sequence. Therefore, in the cultivation of yoga, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* joined together are the general classification of yogas.

III.6.2 However, here for those seeking the yoga of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), four stages of yoga (*yogabhūmi*) must be explained: that which has the limit of things (*vastuparyantatā*) as its object, that which has mind-only (*cittamātra*) as its object, that which has suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, and that which is without an object (*nirālambana*).

Having sent that [consciousness] forth and having set aside the naturally distracted visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses, one—being concentrated and possessing a perception of clear light—should attend to the universe as follows: "This is form (rūpa), such as blue, yellow, and so forth; this is sound (śabda), such as speech, cries, and so forth; this is odor (gandha), such as fragrant, foul, and so forth; this is taste (rasa), such as sweet, sour, and so forth; this is the tangible (spraṣṭavya), such as cold, heat, and so forth; this is the mental object (dharma), such as pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, space, nirvāṇa, and so forth. And of these six objective domains (viṣayadhātu), [one should attend to them] as being objects of apprehension... III.6.2.1.1.

Therein, first, the initial [stage] is described: Here, a bodhisattva endowed with hearing and reflection, having gone alone to a secluded place, sits cross-legged, holding the body straight, neither too slumped nor too rigid, maintaining mindfulness and alertness. The internal forms of light that appear as objects of perception and manifest as subjects of grasping—these are the six consciousness-elements, whose nature is not clearly manifest.

Namely, visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness. And the bases for these six elements of consciousness are the six elements of the sense faculties (*indriyadhātu*). Among them, five consist of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), while one is non-material (*arūpin*); that is to say, the eye is like a star in the center [of the pupil], resembling the *ajājī* flower; the ear at the base of the ears is like a knot in birch bark; and the nose at the base of the nostrils is like a small rod.

The tongue faculty is on the surface of the tongue, like two half-moons separated by a distance the size of a hair-tip. The body faculty is throughout the entire body, like the body itself. The mental faculty element is simply consciousness that has just ceased.

In this way, having brought to mind the eighteen elements—comprised of the six objects, consciousnesses, and faculties of myself and all sentient beings, extending throughout all world-systems in the ten directions—and having taken that very mind appearing as a manifold universe as its object, one should practice tranquility (śamatha) by abandoning mental chatter. The perfection of tranquility is attained upon the acquisition of pliancy (praśrabdhi) of body and mind.

III.6.2.1.2 Then, relying upon calm abiding (*śamatha*), one should accomplish insight (*vipaśyanā*) by extensively analyzing, discerning, thoroughly investigating, and reflecting upon that very same universal image (*viśvapratibimba*), thinking: "This is exactly this much; these are all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), namely the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), from the element of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to the element of mind (*manodhātu*). III.6.2.1.3 [He should accomplish insight] by extensively analyzing, discerning, thoroughly investigating, and reflecting.

Thereafter, with respect to the object of a conceptual reflection, that very mind possesses a continuous flow of mental attention that is equal toward both [calm abiding and insight]; this is the path in which calm abiding and insight proceed yoked together by means of the mind alone.
In the instruction on the perfection of wisdom, the first stage of yoga has as its object the full extent of all that exists.

III.6.2.2.1 Now, for the second [meditation], having likewise produced a mind in which everything appears, one should investigate in this way: "Form is name-only; even the mind is name-only. Thus, all phenomena are name-only. For the name is not the object itself, because they are absolutely distinct. Furthermore, for those who do not understand the object, there is the manifestation of name-only, and for those who do not understand the name, there is the manifestation of object-only. Therefore, since the object does not exist according to its name, form is name-only and not the object."

In this way, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are merely names. Regarding the meaning of "form" (*rūpa*) when it is superimposed upon worldly objects—up to and including "all phenomena"—this is a guest-name superimposed for the sake of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, form does not exist, nor do any phenomena up to and including all phenomena. This is mind-only (*cittamātra*); even though the object does not exist, it arises and appears through the power of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for the appearance of objects and the adherence to objects. It is like the appearance of gambling games arising from the power of practicing gambling.

[The text] breathes forth. In this regard, this adventitious designation has been interpolated for the sake of conventional understanding: "This is mind-only (*cittamātra*); moreover, there is no object whatsoever existing external to the mind that could be grasped by the mind. And when there is no object of grasp (*grāhya*), there can be no grasper (*grāhaka*). Therefore, having ascertained that "this entire universe is indeed mind-only, empty of subject and object, and ineffable," and having abandoned all mental discursive proliferation (*manojalpa*), one should generate calm abiding (*śamatha*) by withdrawing, settling, and making immovable the mind within that very mind-only nature of all phenomena, until [the state of] body and mind...
He attains pliancy.

III.6.2.2.2 Relying precisely upon the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) thus attained, one should repeatedly investigate that very same reflected image which is the domain of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thinking: "This entire universe of eighteen elements is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), mind-only (*cittamātra*), and empty of subject and object (*grāhyagrāhaka*). As he investigates and thoroughly examines it in this way again and again, there arises at that time a bodily and mental pliancy; this is insight (*vipaśyanā*).

III.6.2.2.3 Thereafter, precisely within that very mind—both in the conceptual images and in their objective support—there is a continuous flow of mental attention that is equal toward both. This is calm abiding and insight; it is the path that proceeds by means of the two joined together.
In the instruction on the perfection of wisdom, the second stage of yoga has as its object the mind-only that exists as it truly is.

III.6.2.3.1 [B36.3.1] <Now, the third>: <In the same way>, having produced a mind in which the manifold (*viśva*) appears, one should investigate as follows: "This entire manifold consisting of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), mind-only (*cittamātra*), and empty of the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakaśūnya*). Furthermore, whatever appearance of names here occurs—such as 'form' (*rūpa*), 'sound' (*śabda*), and so forth—"

"5. *Dha* means 'as far as all phenomena (*sarvadharma*)'. That which appears as an object—that is, the appearance of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-fields (*āyatana*), up to the appearance of all phenomena—all this is a sign of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*), because it is a semblance of phenomena. All this is a sign of delusion (*bhrāntinimitta*), a sign of conceptual proliferation (*prapañcanimitta*), and a sign of inversion (*viparyāsanimitta*), because it is the objective support (*ālambana*) of delusion. For cognition arises from that appearance regarding what is non-existent."

It does not appear in that form because it is a distortion; rather, it appears as having that very [object] as its objective support. Therefore, they are called the objective supports of error. Consequently, as long as these continue to appear, there is error—the perception of unreal objects and the non-perception of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Thus, one who wishes to see the ultimate reality of all phenomena should, relying on calm abiding (*śamatha*) in that very same way, completely abandon all signs of error—whether they have become manifest or have entered into appearance—by means of bringing them to non-appearance.

Just as someone, being alone and having gone to a secluded place, might dwell having attained the sphere of infinite space by relying on meditative concentration, through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form and through the presence everywhere of the perception of space; in the same way, this bodhisattva, having concentrated the mind upon the mind that manifests the entire universe of the eighteen elements, and having set aside all mental chatter, should avoid all those signs of delusion and signs of conceptual construction.

That is to say: there are no bodies, no trees, no houses, villages, cities, mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth; no earth, no sky, no light, no darkness, and no moon, sun, planets, constellations, and so forth. Likewise, there is no form whatsoever, nor any sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles. There are no faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, or body, nor any consciousnesses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, or body. There is no mind, no mental consciousness, and no realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Thus, there are no elements (*dhātu*), no sense-bases (*āyatana*), no aggregates (*skandha*), and so on, up to no Buddha-qualities. In this way, having completely abandoned the signs of all phenomena and the signs of all conceptual constructions, because all signs of the apprehended and the dependent signs of the apprehender have subsided, one should perceive the reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena—which is like the solitary, stainless, and infinite sky—as the emptiness of duality and mere luminosity.

And having seen it, one should stabilize the mind within that very mind which is the manifestation of the emptiness of all phenomena; having thus withdrawn it, one should bring calm abiding (*śamatha*) to presence, until there arises pliancy of body and mind.

III.6.2.3.2 15. Then, relying upon that very calm abiding (*śamatha*), one should thus investigate that very same reflection of the emptiness of all phenomena within the sphere of meditative concentration (*samādhi*):

"All these phenomena are neither conjoined nor disjoined; they are formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and possess a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics.
20. Thus it is said.

In this context, "not conjoined" means that they do not exist as having distinct characteristics from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Yet, being real, they appear as if they have become one. "Not disjoined" means that they do not appear with their own distinct individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) either. Rather, it is because the false distinctions of forms—which are conditioned by the conceptualization of the diversity of individual characteristics—do not appear, and because they manifest through the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) known as the ultimate emptiness of duality. Thus, the meaning is that they appear as having a single flavor (*ekarasa*).

And because that ultimate nature transcends the domain of speech and conceptual construction, it cannot be defined by itself and is therefore formless (*arūpin*). Because it cannot be demonstrated to others through words, it is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*). Because it appears like a pure, infinite void, it is unimpeded (*apratigha*). Because it manifests solely as the general characteristic known as emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it has a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); yet even that is its general characteristic.

Nothing other than those [individuals]—neither a real entity in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) nor a negation in the form of a simple exclusion (*prasajyapratiṣedha*)—appears therein, because both of those are impossible. Rather, since those particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are merely adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of false forms within those things whose very essence is manifestation, their non-existence is indeed ultimate. And the non-appearance of those [characteristics] is precisely the appearance of their emptiness. This is exactly what is meant by the phrase "that which is without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇā*).
When, for one who is thus reflecting, deliberating, and investigating thoroughly, there arises pliancy of body and mind, then the perfection of insight (vipaśyanā) is attained.
Between these two is the path that carries the union.

III.6.2.3.3 Thereafter, within that very mind—which possesses conceptualization and consists of the reflection of the emptiness of all phenomena that are the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as its objective support—there arises a continuous, uninterrupted flow of mental attention (*manasikāra*) toward both calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*). This is precisely what is taught in the *Prajñāpāramitā* as "the state of being as it is" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), having the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena as its objective support; this is the third stage of yoga.

III.6.2.4.1.1 For a yogin engaged in the third stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*), as long as even the most subtle conceptualization of phenomena (*dharmavikalpa*) continues to manifest, the third stage is not yet perfected. However, when only the extremely subtle conceptualization of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatāvikalpa*) manifests, it should then be said to be perfected.

III.6.2.4.1.2 Furthermore, when one who is concentrated upon that very same perfected nature (pariniṣpanna) experiences the direct perception of the suchness of all phenomena—by way of effortless spontaneity and without volitional construction—there arises non-conceptual, non-dual, and non-erroneous knowledge through the complete subsiding of the signs of both phenomena and their true nature (dharmatā). This is supramundane, untainted, characterized by non-appearance and lack of objective support, consisting of non-conceptual calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), and possessing an extremely sharp mode of activity.

When right knowledge becomes manifest, that is the fourth stage of yoga. As long as there is no vision of the ultimate truth not yet seen, that is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); but once that which was to be seen has been seen, it is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

III.6.2.4.2 However, the knowledge of suchness (tathatājñāna) subsumed within the third stage is not itself non-conceptual; rather, it is merely the discernment of reality (bhūtapratyavekṣāmātra) which is conducive to the arising of the non-conceptual. This is because one conceptualizes that very suchness by means of it. III.6.2.4.2.1
And so it is said in the *Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī*:
"In this way, that bodhisattva, by means of non-attention (*amanasikāra*), avoids all signs of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as they appear before him and come into manifestation."

By way of not entering into their appearance, one does not yet touch the non-conceptual realm (*avikalpadhātu*). However, there exists this fundamental concentration (*yoniśaḥsamādhi*) for the purpose of touching the non-conceptual realm. Through the sequence of practicing that correct application, through the sequence of cultivation, through the sequence of frequent practice, and through the sequence of correct mental attention, one touches the non-conceptual realm effortlessly and without volitional construction, and gradually purifies it. ||57||

III.6.2.4.2.2 Herein, the "element" (*dhātu*) is non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). "Contact" (*sparśa*) is attainment (*pratilambha*). "Source" (*yoni*) is reality (*tattva*). How is it a source? Because it is the cause by way of being the objective support (*ālambana*). Of what is it the source? It is the source of the noble qualities (*āryadharma*). "Cultivation" (*āsevanā*) is practice according to tradition; it is the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Development" (*bhāvanā*) is proceeding by means of reasoning through one's own being; it is the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Frequent exercise" (*bahulīkāra*) is repeated mental attention (*manasikāra*); it is the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). These three together constitute right mental attention (*samyag-manasikāra*).

The "concomitance" (*anvaya*) of these [perfections] is the establishment, persistence, and continuous succession—like a flowing stream—of the power, strength, or latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) instilled by all of them; this occurs "without effort" (*anābhogataḥ*) and "without volitional construction" (*anabhisaṃskārataḥ*), meaning without the need for separate exertion. "He touches" refers to the stage of *pramuditā* (the Joyous); "gradually" refers to the stages subsequent to that.

Now, what is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of this non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), what is its mark (*liṅga*), and what is its benefit (*anuśaṃsa*)? All three of these have been explained in that very same *dhāraṇī*:

"In this way, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, by not attending to (*amanasikāra*) these signs of conceptualization in all their forms, becomes well-engaged in the non-conceptual; yet he does not for that long touch the non-conceptual realm (*avikalpa-dhātu*)."

However, there is this fundamental concentration for the sake of touching the non-conceptual realm (*avikalpadhātu*). Through the sequence of cultivating that correct application, through the sequence of its frequent practice, and through the sequence of correct mental attention, one touches the non-conceptual realm either by way of being without volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) or by way of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), and one gradually purifies it. III.6.2.4.3.1 Regarding that, first as for the characteristic: how is the non-conceptual realm?

It is called "non-conceptual" because it transcends all conceptualization; because it transcends both the transformation and non-transformation of form, the transcending of teaching and seeing, the transcending of all conceptualizations of the sense faculties, the transcending of all conceptualizations of objects, the transcending of all conceptualizations of representation, and because it is free from any basis for all obscurations. It is non-conceptual, formless, invisible, non-abiding, non-manifest, non-representational, and homeless. (58)
Thus [it is said].

III.6.2.4.3.2 Here, the definition is given by the last seven terms, and their detailed explanation by the preceding seven. "Transcending conceptual constructions" (*vikalpānām atikramaḥ*) occurs because the signs (*nimitta*) of conceptual construction have ceased. In that regard, it is "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*) because it generally transcends all conceptual constructions; this is the brief statement (*uddeśa*). The five [categories] beginning with "form" (*rūpaṇā*) are specific types of conceptual construction. The detailed explanation is by way of transcending them. For here, "form" (*rūpa*) is the act of being formed (*rūpaṇa*), which is itself the process of defining; because one has transcended that, it is "formless" (*arūpa*).

"Teaching" (*deśanā*) is the demonstration through speech, the making known to others; because he has transcended that, he is "without demonstration" (*anidarśana*). The six sense-faculties (*indriya-dhātu*) are the foundation for the designation of a sentient being (*sattva-prajñapti*); because they do not appear [to him], he is "without foundation" (*apratiṣṭha*). That which appears is an "appearance" (*ābhāsa*); the six object-fields (*viṣaya-dhātu*) are appearances. Because they do not appear [to him], he is "without appearance" (*anābhāsa*). Representation (*vijñapti*) consists of the six consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*); because they do not appear [to him], he is "without representation" (*avijñapti*). Thus, first of all, because he has completely transcended all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he is "non-conceptual" (*avikalpa*).

Moreover, because it is the antidote to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), he says that it too is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). "Without abode" (*aniketa*): an abode (*niketa*) is a dwelling (*ālaya*), the place where conceptual constructions comprised within the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) reside. That [abode] does not exist there, because they have been abandoned by that very antidote. Therefore, it is without abode; for that reason also, it is non-conceptual.
III.6.2.4.3.3 Now, he states the sign that occurs upon its attainment:

A bodhisattva established in the non-conceptual realm perceives all phenomena as equal to space by means of a gnosis that is indistinguishable from the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Subsequently, through the gnosis obtained after that, he perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion, a mirage, a dream, a reflection, an echo, a mirror-image, the moon in water, and a magical creation. 59.
Thus:

III.6.2.4.3.4 Here, that very supramundane gnosis (*lokottarajñāna*), which is non-distinct from the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), is without differentiation regarding all phenomena that are objects of knowledge, because it perceives only suchness (*tathatā*) as a single flavor. A-

Alternatively, they are indistinguishable from the object of knowledge because they consist of mere suchness (*tathatāmātra*), since they possess a single flavor (*ekarasa*). Alternatively, they are indistinguishable and non-different from the object of knowledge as mere suchness, because they appear without any separation from it. This is because, having taken suchness as the grasped object, they do not appear as its grasper; thus, the signs of the dharma and the dharmin have set. "Level like space" means level like space. They are "level" (*samatala*) because their entire surface (*tala*) is equally without obstruction.

By means of that which is obtained subsequent to it—namely, by pure mundane knowledge obtained through the power of supramundane [wisdom]—one perceives the world of sentient beings there as being like an illusion, because it appears through unreal forms such as women and men; the receptacle world as being like a mirage, because it appears falsely through the nature of water and so forth; the enjoyment of sense objects as being like a dream, because it lacks any real substance; and bodily action as being like a reflection, because it is devoid of movement.

Vocal action is like an echo, because it is devoid of intrinsic sound. Mental action belonging to the level of non-concentration is like a reflection in a mirror, because although the object does not exist, only a reflection of the object appears therein. Mental action belonging to the level of concentration is like the moon in water, because it is moistened by the water of serenity (*praśrabdhi*). Mental action produced by another is seen as being like a magical creation (*nirmita*), because it is dependent upon another.
III.6.2.4.3.5 Now, regarding the benefit that arises from its attainment, he states it briefly in a single verse and in detail through a single summary:
"It is peaceful, immovable, and supreme."
It is sovereign, equal to the unequaled;
therefore, the bodhisattva attains non-conceptual bliss.
Thus [ends] the verse.

III.6.2.4.3.6 Herein, it is "tranquil" because it is free from afflictions (*niṣkleśatva*). It is "immovable" because it is not subject to decline. It is "supreme" because it is more distinguished than other forms of happiness. It is "masterful" because it can be brought into manifestation at will and for as long as one desires. It is "equal" to other forms of happiness by virtue of being of the same genus; yet it is also "unequal" to them by these very four distinctions—thus it is both equal and unequal. "Therefore" means from non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpajñāna*).

Greatness consists in being mental and vast. A "dwelling" (*vihāra*) is so called because one dwells by means of that meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The "fulfillment of mind" (*cittasamṛddhi*) refers to the formless absorptions (*ārūpya*) and so forth. "Teaching" (*deśanā*) is the proclamation of the Dharma. "Purposeful activity" (*arthakriyā*) refers to the subduing of afflictions and so forth. "Vastness" (*vaipulyatā*) is the mastery over these very things.
In the instruction on the Perfection of Wisdom, the fourth stage of yoga is the non-appearance.
III.6.3.1 Furthermore, this realization was taught by the Blessed One in three verses in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*:
"Having ascended to mind-only, one should not conceptualize external objects."
Abiding with suchness as the object of focus, one should transcend mind-only;
having transcended mind-only,
one should transcend the appearanceless.
The yogi established in the signless beholds the Mahāyāna;
his effortless course is peaceful.
Purified by aspirational prayers,
one perceives through the Mahāyāna the supreme, selfless gnosis. (64)
Thus [it is said].
III.6.3.2 It is also stated in the glorious *Guhyasamāja* with a single verse:
"In the contemplation of one's own mind, all phenomena are established; for these phenomena abide in the space-vajra."
5. There are neither phenomena nor the nature of phenomena. ||65||

III.6.3.3.1 In both cases, the first stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*) is stated by implication. This is because the emptiness of all phenomena is difficult to penetrate as long as their full extent has not been fathomed. For instance: the delimitation of the full extent of all phenomena constitutes the first stage of yoga. The resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the very nature of those same phenomena as being "mind-only" and empty of duality, yet accompanied by appearances (*sābhāsa*), is the second. Within that same state, the light of resolute conviction that is free from appearances (*nirābhāsa*) due to the signs of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*), which is like a vision, is the third.
The fourth [insight] is the vision that is absolutely without appearance, due to all the signs of both phenomena and their true nature within that very [state].

III.6.3.3.2.1 In this context, "mind-only" refers to the knowledge that has mind-only as its object; the meaning is that this is the second stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*). "One should not conceptualize" means that one should transcend both that conceptualization, which is the nature of the first stage of yoga, and any other [conceptualization]. "Knowledge that has suchness as its object" means that suchness is the objective support (*ālambana*); the meaning is that this is the third stage of yoga.
III.6.3.3.2.2 “Having transcended mind-only” (*cittamātram atikramya*) is a restatement of what has already been said, not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

“He should transcend the non-manifest” (*nirābhāsam atikramet*) is an original injunction. Here, “non-manifest” (*nirābhāsa*) means being non-manifest with respect to the signs of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*), that is, having suchness as its objective support (*tathatālambana*). How should he transcend? By abiding in the non-manifest. That is to say, by abiding in a vision that is absolutely non-manifest with respect to the signs of both phenomena and their true nature (*dharmadharmatānimitta*); the meaning is that he does so while established in the fourth stage of yoga (*yogabhūmi*). The term “the yogi” (*yogī*) should also be connected to the preceding statements.

The word "he" refers to the yogin established on the fourth stage of yoga who perceives the Mahāyāna. That by which one goes is a "vehicle" (yāna), meaning a path. Because it is distinguished from the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the Mahāyāna is the untainted path of the Bodhisattvas. He perceives this; that is, he realizes it directly. Therefore, that very gnosis is the Mahāyāna.

III.6.3.3.2.3 Now, what is the destination by means of that Mahāyāna, or what does he go to by means of it? To this, he speaks the third verse: "The effortless movement" (*anābhoga-gati*) refers to proceeding in such a manner without effort on the supramundane stages (*bhūmi*). It is "peaceful" (*śāntā*) because of the absence of afflictions (*niṣkleśatva*) and the absence of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*). It is "purified by vows" (*praṇidhāna-viśodhitā*) for the purpose of preventing a fall into inferior enlightenment. The "movement" has been explained. "Knowledge is selfless" (*jñānaṃ nirātmakam*) because it is absolutely without appearance (*atyanta-nirābhāsatva*). It is "supreme" (*śreṣṭha*) because of the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsana-sarvāvaraṇa-prahāṇa*).
The meaning is "the awakening of a Buddha. By means of that Mahāyāna, that yogi sees, realizes, and goes [to it]; such is the meaning.

III.6.3.3.3 The second stage is the mental realization (*cittanidhyapti*). Established in it, all phenomena appear as one’s own mind, because of the certainty that "this [world] of mine is only my own mind; though duality does not exist, it appears as duality. The third stage is when, in the space-vajra which is free from the appearance of duality, none of the phenomena (*dharma*) nor even their true nature (*dharmatā*) appear while remaining therein; therein, the forms of phenomena do not appear. The fourth stage is when even the forms of the true nature of phenomena do not appear.
Verses on the Clear Realization in the Instruction on the Perfection of Wisdom.

III.7 By propagating this *Prajñāpāramitā*— which is fundamental, as stainless as the sky, and likewise consisting of the wisdom derived from reflection, meditation, and hearing, beginning with that which is acquired through application—
whatever merit has been attained by me, may it lead me to the state of a Sugata; and may all these people of diverse dispositions emerge by means of the three vehicles.
IV.
The instruction on the perfection of wisdom is completed.
